#6077. Review: Air France A350-900 Business Class Paris To New York

Air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to New York. The new A350-900 cabin is excellent, but what impressed me most was how well everything came together, from the comfortable seat to the delicious dinner, gracious service, and fast Starlink Wi-Fi.

I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe. Having had more time to reflect on it, I stand by that assessment…this flight left very little room for improvement.

I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer. Flying Blue came through with a last-minute business class award from Basel to Paris to New York for 60,000 miles plus €453 in taxes and fees. The timing worked perfectly and I booked this about 36-hour before departure, so saver space can certainly open up via FlyingBlue.

This was a so-called “reverse redeye,” leaving Europe late in the evening and arriving in the United States even later that same evening. That suited my plans very well, particularly because I had an overnight drive to Pittsburgh ahead of me after landing.

My journey began in Basel with an Air France Hop! flight to Paris. I had time to visit the lounge before my connection and enjoyed a meal there, though I deliberately left room for dinner onboard.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 6L. Though approaching 8:00 pm, it was still very light outside.

I first reviewed Air France A350 business class in 2020, flying from Paris to Toronto. I enjoyed that flight very much, but the newer business class cabin represents a substantial improvement.

Far more important the gimmicky door was the room for your feet, which I found plentiful. Legroom is 43 inches when the seat is the upright position and it transforms into a bed that is 79 inches long. Seats are 21 inches wide.

There are no personal art vents, but thankfully the cabin was kept very chilly. I also loved the window darkening feature, where the window tinting could be adjusted simply by sliding your finger left or right.

I found this suite spacious and comfortable whether sitting upright, reclining, or lying down. The cabin looks so sharp. I particularly love the illuminated winged seahorse at each seat…a small detail, but one that gives the cabin an unmistakable Air France identity.

There was plenty of personal storage, and the wireless charging worked well, though there was also USB-C and universal A/C power.

After dinner, I converted my seat into a bed and slept for about four hours.

The Sofitel-branded bedding (duvet, mattress pad, pillow) was excellent, and I found the seat very comfortable for sleeping.

This is one of my favorite business class seats.

Air France provided a very attractive amenity kit with an embossed seahorse on the bag. It was lined with red and the contents included:

The catering was a highlight of this flight. I had eaten in the lounge, but was very glad I saved room for dinner.

Before takeoff, flight attendants offered Champagne and a warm towel, along with the familiar Gavottes savory biscuits.

The full menu (every menu item and ingredient is French except for Coca-Cola):

Dinner began with an appetizer of pea, lemon, and basil cream accompanied by smoked salmon fillet and raspberry and grapefruit jelly.

A side salad accompanied the starter, though I saved mine until after the main course, as the French do. The bread was delicious.

I also tried the Quintessence cocktail, an Air France variation on a Negroni. It combined La Quintinye royal red vermouth, bitter Chambéry liqueur, a hint of fig, and ABK6 VSOP Cognac. I enjoyed it very much. It was not nearly as strong as a traditional Negroni, which suited me just fine on this flight.

For my main course, I chose veal with a creamy morel mushroom sauce, spelt risotto, and peas.

Admittedly, the presentation was not going to win any awards…yes, it looked like vomit. But it tasted delicious and I would happily order it again. I enjoyed a delicious glass of Chateau D’Arsac wine, which was so good.

A cheese course followed, then dessert. I enjoyed both ice cream and a crispy hazelnut tart, accompanied by hot chocolate.

This was a substantial supper and a very satisfying one.

About an hour before landing, flight attendants served a light meal of shrimp with a pickled cucumber salad.

It was excellent and just the right amount of food after the large dinner. I had two espressos with it, which helped prepare me for the late night ahead.

The entertainment system included a tail camera, which I particularly enjoyed during our departure from Paris (though not the fire that seemed to be burning near CDG). It was a gorgeous evening, and watching the aircraft leave Charles de Gaulle was a lovely way to begin the flight.

I did not watch any movies or TV on this flight, but there was large selection of movies, TV shows, games, and music.

Noise-cancelling headphones were provided, though you can also connect your own Bluetooth device.

Fast, free Starlink internet was available onboard. The connection worked from gate to gate and felt much like using the internet on the ground. I did not have any essential work to complete on this flight, but I appreciated being able to connect onboard. Starlink increasingly influences which flights I book. Air France already gives me plenty of reasons to choose it, but reliable internet makes the proposition even more attractive, especially for a daytime westbound journey when I might otherwise spend several hours working.

The Air France A350 has three lavatories in business class: one I the front (though typically reserved for crew use) and two in between the front and rear cabin.

Service was warm and attentive throughout the flight. I was even addressed by surname.

I have heard plenty of complaints over the years about service on Air France, but my own experiences have been very positive. This crew continued that pattern and the great service complemented the rest of the experience. I enjoyed a delicious meal, slept comfortably, and felt well cared for throughout the journey.

The new seat deserves attention, but a cabin can only do so much without a good crew in terms of leaving a lasting positive impression. On this flight, Air France delivered both.

We landed on time at JFK, and I quickly cleared immigration using Global Entry. The late arrival had been part of the appeal when booking, and the flight delivered exactly what I had hoped for: an enjoyable evening onboard, a few hours of rest, and an on-time arrival in New York.

Then it was time to collect a rental car and begin my overnight drive to Pittsburgh…

This was a tremendous flight on Air France…I have no complaints at all about anything.

I liked the older A350 business class product when I flew it in 2020, but the newer seat is a considerable improvement. Pair that with excellent bedding, delicious food, and a gracious crew, then add Starlink, and I struggle to identify much that I would change. Cappuccinos maybe that are not powdered?

The lack of individual air vents remains a drawback, though the comfortable cabin temperature thankfully meant it did not interfere with my sleep on this flight.

Air France reminded me how enjoyable a transatlantic business class flight can be when the airline gets the details right. I would happily book this product again and would go out of my way to find it.

#6076. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#6075. How We Pulled It Off: A Pakistani Wedding Under the Mudéjar Arches of Seville

An incredible love story deserves an incredible wedding. Growing up in the Atlanta suburbs, Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a field trip in middle school, then became best friends as teenagers. It was toward the end of high school that their connection turned romantic.

“She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered. “We decided to see where things would take us.”

Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.

The two grew up in the Atlanta area and got together toward the end of high school.

The relationship took them into their twenties through to a proposal in July 2023: an elaborate scavenger hunt that Awaez staged around Chicago, where they lived briefly before turning to Atlanta. When plotting their wedding, they were sure they wanted something just as detailed and thoughtful, and immediately landed on a destination celebration. “We knew we didn’t want to have it in Atlanta, because we didn’t feel like we would be able to give our guests the kind of intentional experience we really wanted to,” says Falaknaz.

Ahead, the couple explains how and why they chose to hold a Seville destination wedding in August 2025 for 160 guests, and discusses the (many!) venues they booked for their various events, the fun guest surprise they plotted, and loads of other sangria-soaked details.

Hotel Alfonso XIII is an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for the Spanish king.

The property and Sevilla in general are known for the Mudéjar-style architecture of Southern Spain.

Falaknaz and Awaez were open to getting married anywhere, a wonderful but intimidating prospect. They scoured Pinterest and spoke to planners across the US. “We looked into Chicago, we looked into California, and at one point we looked into a cabin wedding in Montana,” the bride says. “None of those really felt right until I came across some of the venues in Seville, Spain.”

Her major moment of connection was seeing the Hotel Alfonso XIII, an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for a king of Spain, who aimed to host esteemed international guests there. The scale and vibe of Seville itself—smaller than other European cities, but with an incredible history, stunning architecture, and loads to do—appealed as well. The couple reached out to several planners and booked a trip to visit the Alfonso and several other venues.

In person, the property was just as incredible as they’d hoped. “Hotel Alfonso was honestly a non-negotiable for me once we stayed there that very first trip,” says Awaez. “We were exposed to all the different ways we could utilize the hotel and make the most of it.”

And given the hotel’s 150 rooms, the majority of their guest list could stay there, and did. “One of the major things we wanted from the wedding was everyone to be together. We loved the idea of it being almost a resort, where you’re constantly bumping into people from the wedding,” says Falaknaz.

The couple chose event-planning firm Bodas del Sur because it had worked on South Asian weddings before.

As they tried to narrow down the location for their wedding, the couple had a few dismaying calls with potential event firms. “We met with a lot of planners, and they had a lot of stipulations right off the bat. They weren't really open to hearing what we wanted out of our wedding,” Falaknaz says. They ultimately opted to work with Bodas del Sur, a Seville-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Andalusia and gave them utter confidence in their ideas. “From our very first conversation, they just seemed like they were going to make what we wanted happen,” the bride continues. “Whatever we said, they ran with it, like, ‘Okay, these are all the ways we can make it happen.’ That was the most reassuring thing: that we felt heard.”

In addition to their vast experience with Seville venues and vendors, Bodas del Sur had also worked on South Asian weddings in the past, says the bride, “so it gave us a lot of confidence that they knew what they were doing.”

A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

A key aspect of the typical South Asian wedding is that it involves several events, and for the couple’s own Muslim-Pakistani celebration, they figured out quickly that not all of them made sense for the Hotel Alfonso XIII. Though Falaknaz began to panic at the realization—“Of course I was like, all hope is lost, we have to go back to the drawing board”—the Bodas team took them to see more spaces, which cemented Seville for them as a whole.

“The first venue they took us to was Casa de Pilatos. We both walked in and were like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is it. We can’t possibly give this up,’” Falaknaz says. “And the more places they took us to, the more we fell in love with Seville.” The biggest draw for the couple was the city’s rich Islamic heritage—it was under Muslim rule for over 500 years—and the corresponding architectural features, such as the arches, pillars, and intricate tiles, a fusion with Christian motifs known as Mudéjar style.

A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th century formerly private home known for its iconic Sevillian architecture.

“That blend was something we just weren’t finding elsewhere,” says Falaknaz. “That’s truly where we felt like we could give our guests the kind of experience we wanted—that would make them feel connected to something that was more than just a wedding.”

The couple held four major events over three days. The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th-century formerly private home commissioned by a nobleman that stands as an apex of Sevillian Romantic architecture. The pithi, another daytime party during which the couple is decorated with turmeric paste to represent a pre-wedding cleansing as well as the golden joy to come, was staged at Hotel Alfonso XIII. The night of dancing and performances, also known as the sangeet, happened at Casa de Pilatos, while the slightly more Western-style wedding reception and its after-party were at Hacienda La Soledad, an estate constructed in 1542 as the center of an olive grove.

The Sevilla celebration of 160 people felt “tiny” compared to the Atlanta nuptials the couple held for their legal ceremony.

The one ceremony the couple didn’t have on site in Spain? The actual wedding itself. Their Nikkah, the Islamic wedding rites, was held at an Ismaili Jamatkhana at home in Atlanta, in an effort to include the much larger guest list of everyone important to their families, about 600 people in all. That contributed to the relatively tiny group of 160 in Seville feeling much more intimate—“Well, intimate was still about 160, but intimate for us,” says Falaknaz.

“We felt connected to doing that in a place where we both grew up. We were able to do it in our mosque at home, the one we grew up going to and where all of our friends and parents’ community is. It was really special to have that be a part of the storyline, that we’ll share hopefully when we have kids,” says Falaknaz. “It was nice to be able to share that with everyone that wouldn't be able to make it to Spain.”

The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender cala lilies and pearl chandeliers.

Given the spectacular aesthetics of their chosen venues, the couple decided to bring in very little outside decor, and keep what they did bring in complementary. “The intention was to find places that spoke for themselves,” says Awaez. “We wouldn’t have to dedicate so much time to constructing the decor, versus the place standing on its own.”

For their first two events, they matched the color schemes to the major activities, with the pithi blanketed in shades of turmeric (from fluffy roses to mirrored pillows), and the mehendi outfitted in reddish browns and burnt orange. To create the feeling of intimacy and home at the latter, tables and other furniture were kept low, and wide cushions lay on a floor covered in overlapping rugs to encourage lounging.

Their sangeet was a night filled with dance performances, channeling a peacock theme to echo the jewel-toned florals and vivid garden colors.

Their sangeet, the night filled with dance performances, fittingly received a peacock theme, which carried from the feathers embroidered on Falaknaz’s gold gown by Taali to the signage to a jewel-toned palette for the florals. “We pulled colors that we felt would balance the venue, with these beautiful blues in the tiling and obviously the greens in the gardens,” says Falaknaz, who changed into a glittering indigo lehenga by Seema Gujral for her own performance.

The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender calla lilies and pearl chandeliers, with architectural floral sculptures set around a fountain. Their planners were the key minds behind the creative vibe of the wedding, along with a local florist, La Galería by Jesús Fuertes.

Transportation to the sangeet was by horse-drawn carriage, and the couple's photography sessions included a ride around Seville's iconic Plaza de España.

While the schedule (and culture) of the wedding events was very expected, the couple kept guests on their toes when it came to transportation to the sangeet: They were taken by horse-drawn carriages to Casa de Palatos. “They were so surprised to see a whole bunch of carriages waiting outside for us. It was such a cool moment,” says Awaez. The rides took a scenic route through the Plaza de España before reaching the venue. “We knew that our guests probably weren't going to be able to have a lot of downtime between the events to explore the city,” says Falaknaz of the bonus tour.

Falaknaz wore a glittering lehenga by Seema Gujral.

While much of dinner was Desi dishes, the couple also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella.

A key part of Awaez and Falaknaz’s three planning trips to Seville involved considering the caterers that their planners suggested. “We were genuinely concerned about how the food was going to taste, especially out in Spain in comparison to our typical Indian-Pakistani restaurants here in the U.S.,” says Awaez. “We tested and tried a lot of those options that they shared with us, and found several of our own, and ultimately the two that we landed on were fantastic.” They worked with the staff of the Indian restaurant Taj Mahal Sevilla to cater their sangeet, and Ágape 360 Catering y Eventos for their mehendi and reception.

The gastronomic director of Ágape 360, Manuel de Pablo Deco, is Spanish but was excited to learn and adapt to the couple’s cultural needs: For a few crucial dishes, among them Desi-style karahi paneer and a nihari beef stew, the couple’s mothers actually found YouTube videos demonstrating the technique for cooking the recipes. “We sent those videos over to Manu, and he studied them to a T. He really learned to cook Indian food from scratch,” says the grateful bride.

After days of distinctly Pakistani events, the couple’s wedding reception was an unabashed celebration of the local culture. Tinto de verano, a popular summery version of sangria, was served at the cocktail hour, while passed hors d’oeuvres included tapas bites like torta de potatas, Moorish-spiced meat skewers, and chicken croquettes. A troupe of flamenco dancers performed; the couple had seen the group dance at a taverna their planners had recommended on their first planning trip to Seville. While much of their dinner was Desi dishes, they also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella, in both seafood and vegetarian styles—followed by flan for dessert.

To create the feeling of intimacy, tables and florals were kept low.

A step and repeat served as a photo op for guests to snap their own shots.

To maximize their booking and the guest experience alike, Falaknaz and Awaez utilized each possible room or space within their venues. For the sangeet, they took family and couple portraits in the gardens of the Casa de Pilatos, moved to the central, most ornate courtyard for dinner and speeches, held performances in the soaring “courtyard of the halt,” and then moved to an entirely inner room for the after-party, given the local ordinance in the city center that required outdoor spaces to quiet down after 11:00 pm.

In order to keep the energy high for that final transition, they enlisted the help of their bridal party, who performed the final dance act of the night. “Almost flash mob style, we ran off the stage and through the crowd and into the indoor space,” says Falaknaz. The same crowd-pleasing song that’d been playing outside was already being piped indoors— “Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje,” from the beloved Bollywood movie Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam—so the group of 100+ party-goers was enticed to stay a little longer. Or a lot longer: The party continued back at the hotel’s basement, stretching until 3:00 am.

The couple invited friends to join them after the wedding for a trip to La Tomatina in Valencia.

The end of the trip afforded more one-on-one time with guests than the busy wedding weekend.

Wedding events took place Friday through Monday, and most guests left on Tuesday, though plenty decided to extend their trip on either end. The newlyweds themselves decided to attend La Tomatina festival in Valencia, in which festival-goers eat but also pelt each other with tomatoes—otherwise known as the biggest food fight in the world. They threw out an invitation for any interested guests to join them, and more than 30 wound up attending.

“It was really special to be able to decompress after the wedding with so many of our friends, and actually have more quality time with them than we did at the wedding,” says Falaknaz. And it turned out to be a suitably colorful ending for an unforgettable wedding celebration.

One of the top premium cards, the offers many lifestyle-centered benefits and statement credits. Those include several health- and fitness-centered benefits, including an Oura Ring statement credit for up to $200 per calendar year (enrollment is required).

With the end of the calendar year fast approaching, now's a good time to decide whether you can use this credit before it resets.

Here's how this statement credit works and whether it makes sense for you.

One of the many lifestyle statement credits available through the is up to $200 each calendar year toward Oura Ring. Specifically, the statement credit applies to hardware purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. (Enrollment is required.)

The Oura Ring is a wearable, health-tracking smart ring. Some key data it tracks includes:

Imagine an Apple Watch or Fitbit, but in ring form. Oura currently sells the Oura Ring 4 starting at $349 and the newer Oura Ring 5 starting at $399. While this statement credit won't fully cover the cost of a ring, it will get you more than halfway there.

One notable advantage of the Oura Ring is that you don't have to charge it as often as other wearables — the Oura Ring 5 typically lasts six or more days on a full charge.

Related: The best credit cards to maximize fitness spending

Amex states that the statement credit should post within eight weeks, but some TPG staffers have seen it post within days.

If you're trying to use this statement credit before Dec. 31, don't wait for the last minute. Amex relies on the date Oura processes the transaction, which might be a day or two after you place the order.

This is particularly important if you order a sizing kit: The ring itself won't process and ship until you confirm your size in your Oura account. Place your order now to get things started.

Related: Why the new Amex Platinum changes are converting me to a cardmember

This statement credit is a more niche perk that not all cardmembers will be able to use. For starters, many people may prefer other forms of wearables. If health data doesn't interest you, this statement credit won't move the needle either.

Plus, the fact that this statement credit doesn't cover the full cost of the ring may also deter some cardmembers. The out-of-pocket cost will still run you at least $149, unless you land a good sale. You'll also need to pay for an Oura Membership at $5.99 monthly or $69.99 per year.

I hope Amex expands this statement credit to cover a subscription in the future, since it's needed to fully maximize your Oura Ring's features.

Even if Oura Ring is of interest, you may not want to buy a new one every year, meaning some years the benefit may go unused.

If you don't think you’d use the statement credit yourself, you could gift a ring to one of your health- and fitness-minded friends or family members.

It's also important to note that this is a shared statement credit, meaning authorized users do not receive their own.

This sole statement credit shouldn't be the deciding factor on whether you add this card to your wallet, but if you can use it organically, it can help recoup some of the Platinum's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Related: Complete guide to authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card

The Oura Ring statement credit can be valuable for Platinum Card members who already plan to buy a fitness tracker, especially if they can stack it with a sale. However, you might find it smarter to let the statement credit go unused some or all years.

However, it would be ideal if this statement credit were expanded in the future to cover the subscription cost, as this would make it more accessible for more cardmembers to use year after year.

#6073. L.L.Bean Promo Code | 60% Off | Black Friday 2026

If there's one thing L.L.Bean is going to do, it's stand the test of time. The quintessentially American outdoor brand supplies everything from hunting shoes and field coats to wool sweaters and flannel sheets—all made with exceptional quality. Whether you're fly-fishing in Montana, camping in the Great Smoky Mountains, or holed up in a cabin somewhere in the Hudson Valley, L.L.Bean has the gear you need to feel at one with nature. And stocking up on the essentials doesn't have to break the bank; there's always a sale, promotion, or coupon code within reach.

Founded in 1912 by Leon Leonwood Bean, L.L.Bean started out as a purveyor of the Maine Hunting Shoe, from a one-room operation in Freeport, Maine. The brand first expanded internationally in 1992 with a store in Japan, and today, some of its most popular items have reached cult status. Take the Boat and Tote, for example. Originally launched as a bag to haul ice and wood in 1944, the iconic tote is often sold out, leading to vintage markups on Ebay and designer spin-offs. Whether you're a seasoned hiker or an it-girl who just wants to get in on the canvas tote trend, read on for the best ways to save at L.L.Bean this Black Friday.

When you register for L.L.Bean's newsletter—where you'll find regular updates on the latest arrivals, upcoming sales, and exclusive coupons—you'll get 10% off your first order, delivered to your email within an hour or two after signing up. Newsletter signees will also be treated to free shipping on orders of $75 and more.

For Black Friday, the retailer is offering 15% off your purchase with code GIFT15. Now's the time to get that Boat and Tote, a can't-go-wrong gift for just about anyone. This coupon code also applies to the daily refreshment of new deals, so you can end up saving up to 60% or more on your favorite styles, like this Popham puffer jacket for women, or this West Branch fishing shirt for men. Sales on shoes and camping gear are listed every day from 6 a.m. to midnight ET, like this do-it-all puffer blanket that's now 17% off. When it comes to clothing, you'll find new deals posted every day at both 6 a.m. and 2 p.m. ET. Whether you're looking to purchase a cozy PJ set, a quarter-zip pullover, or performance flannel, take advantage of this extra discount on top of clearance prices.

L.L.Bean gives thanks to those who have served our country, medical professionals, first responders, students, and teachers. If you are an active, veteran, or retired military personnel (or a family member of one), simply upload an official government-issued documentation with your name, branch of service, and current military status to receive 10% off future orders. Medical professionals and first responders—including police, firefighters, EMTs, and search and rescue workers—can receive the same discount of 10% off. After verifying name, school name, and date showing current enrollment status, college students and teachers can also get a 10% discount.

If you're a tried and true fan of the beloved outdoor brand, consider opening an L.L.Bean Mastercard. You'll get a 25% off coupon once you're approved, and can earn ‘Bean Bucks’ to use on future purchases: The rewards structure offers 4% for L.L.Bean purchases, 2% for restaurants, and 1% for all other purchases. There's no annual fee attached to the card, and 1 Bean Buck translates to $1 in future savings. Cardholders can enjoy a few other perks, too, like free shipping and monogramming.

It has been a messy few weeks for air travel in the U.S., and unfortunately, it appears the Thanksgiving rush could bring another big wave of flight delays.

Storm systems developing along both coasts threaten to disrupt holiday plans for travelers catching last-minute flights, though few major problems have been reported (so far). Fewer than 70 Wednesday flights had been canceled as of 6:20 p.m. EST, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. About 5,000 were delayed, though there were few major trouble spots. Flight data firm Cirium estimated that about 27,000 flights were scheduled for the U.S. for the day.

However, about 120 of Thursday's flights had been preeemptively canceled, with about half of those coming at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Boston's Logan International Airport (BOS) ahead of a strong coastal storm expected to arrive to the region in the morning. The total of Thursday's preempetive cancellations at doubled since earlier Wednesday afternoon, foretelling bigger problems for the Northeast. Travelers there should keep an eye on their flight status if they're schedule to fly on Thanksgiving day.

More broadly, the nation's four biggest airlines had rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions. (Details below.)

On the West Coast, heavy rain and wind are forecast to move into the Pacific Northwest just as travel peaks on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, forecasters are warning of a “monster” storm that could disrupt flights at several of the nation’s busiest East Coast hubs on Wednesday and Thursday.

Further, a new round of storms in South Florida and possible wintry weather in St. Louis added to the mix.

“The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen told TPG.

It’s looking like the latest in a series of frustrations for flyers. In the past two weeks alone, travelers dealt with a nationwide ground stop that led to 18,000 flight cancellations as well as technology outages at United and Delta Air Lines.

Now, it appears Mother Nature will be the biggest obstacle during one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

The West Coast storm is expected to impact the Thanksgiving getaway, although by 7 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the worst of the rainfall appeared to have passed.

Late Monday, United issued a travel advisory for its San Francisco hub amid concerns that high tides could cause flooding at the airport.

Fortunately, Bay Area leaders are no longer worried about flooding at the airport itself.

In recent days, forecasters had grown concerned that heavy rain and high tides could lead to water covering SFO’s taxiways, which are right next to San Francisco Bay.

“At this moment, we are not expecting flood water to reach onto the tarmac at SFO, which is a positive development,” San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said in a social media post — while warning that ground stops because of weather conditions were “still a possibility.”

In a statement to TPG on Tuesday, SFO officials said the airport was keeping pump stations and drainage areas clear, and staging sandbags ahead of the forecast bad weather.

A storm system moves into Washington and Oregon on Wednesday, with locally heavy rain forecast for areas around both Portland and Seattle.

That storm is forecast to last through at least Friday, and although airlines have not issued travel waivers — suggesting they don't expect the storm to be too impactful on their operations — it would still be wise to anticipate possible delays if you're traveling.

The worst travel disruptions, however, could come from a powerful coastal storm developing in the east, meteorologists warn.

That East Coast system could bring strong winds, heavy rain and flooding to a large swath of the coast — including many of the nation’s busiest airports, according to Van Dillen.

He laid out which airports could be heavily affected:

“My advice would be, the earlier you can get to your destination, the better,” Van Dillen advised East Coast travelers.

As of Wednesday morning, the storm was affecting much of the Southeast with locally heavy rain, according to The Weather Channel.

But on Thursday and into Thursday night, the storm is expected to move up to the Northeast, with heavy rain, strong winds and possibly freezing in some areas.

The remnants of the storm could cause lasting delays into Friday, before it peters out by Saturday.

We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

All of the major airlines are offering travel waivers for those flying to, from or through Northeast airports on Thursday, so you may want to consider taking advantage of that if your plans allow.

While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself is typically one of the quietest days of the year at airports.

All eyes will be on how Mother Nature cooperates on Saturday and Sunday, as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

More 2026 Thanksgiving travel coverage from TPG:

Here are some things you should do if you're planning to fly in the next few days.

Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

Have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:

Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

#6071. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

#6070. This Cruise Proves the Congo is No Heart of Darkness—Or Viral Fad

Occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

A floating village in the Congo River Basin

The idea could be said to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading company. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”

The latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

In comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

“Don’t worry,” our guide said. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

Eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

In the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

The Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

One night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

#6069. Norse Atlantic Says Financial Situation ‘Critical’

After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways said Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.

The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the months since the war started, the airline has cut staff, furloughed some crew members, suspended unprofitable routes, and instituted temporary pay reductions for some non-flying crew, but these steps have apparently not put Norse Atlantic back on solid ground.

“[The company’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials said in a statement. “Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover.”

“Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution,” the message continued. “Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”

Rising fuel costs have set back airlines around the world, but the squeeze is arguably worst in Europe, since the continent depends mainly on Gulf oil and has little domestic refining capacity. The crisis has forced Latvia’s airBaltic into bankruptcy, teed up EasyJet’s sale to Apollo Global Management, and inflicted considerable damage on Lufthansa’s core brand.

It was not immediately clear if Norse Atlantic has any candidates in mind for a potential merger. The carrier is not part of any global airline alliance, though it partners with operators such as EasyJet, Norwegian Air Shuttle, and Pegasus through its Norse Connections program.

Bloomberg reported in 2023 and 2024 that the carrier was weighing alliances with larger airlines, possibly through an equity stake, but none were named.

Norse Atlantic operates only long-haul flights. Its network has been adjusted multiple times over the last year in an effort to reduce costs.

#6068. China Southern Orders 50 737 MAX Jets

A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.

The airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian. Deliveries are expected from 2031 to 2034.

The deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

President Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

Trump said earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

China Southern said the new aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.

#6067. The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.)

The kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

Definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

There are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

The longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

The rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

While Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

This is one of the best times of the year to find flight deals. Black Friday is almost here, followed quickly by Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday. All the major airlines, hotels and booking platforms have big sales. Of course, TPG will have roundups of all the best deals, but there are other ways to find deals that I've been experimenting with: artificial intelligence.

I've been an AI skeptic the past few years, at least when it comes to finding and booking travel deals, but it has come a long way since TPG tried to use AI to plan an itinerary back in 2023. (Spoiler: It didn't do a great job.)

But the technology has improved significantly over the past few years, especially when it comes to confirming you are getting a good deal.

ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Google Gemini can now also help you compare prices and find cheaper airports or travel dates, decipher fare rules and restrictions, and even let you know whether it's better to pay cash or use points or miles.

I still don't find AI great at finding mileage or points awards, but it can do a lot.

"AI is already a powerful tool for finding flight deals and only getting better, but it’s still got a long way to go," Thrifty Traveler executive editor Kyle Potter said. "It’s prone to mistakes and falls victim to phantom award availability."

Still, combining AI with tools like Google Flights and Points Path can make finding deals easier and potentially save you some serious money (or miles).

So it can be a useful tool, but I don’t think it’ll ever be the only tool travelers need.

Here are some ways to use AI to find deals.

Like I always tell people looking for deals, flexibility is key. Rather than asking for a specific date or flight, describe your budget, home airport, ideal travel dates and how flexible you are in your AI tool.

AI will work with tools like Google Flights to help you find a good deal. Here's a sample prompt:

"I'm looking for Black Friday flight deals departing from New York City. My budget is $500 round-trip, I'm flexible on destinations, and I can travel between January and March 2027. Suggest 10 destinations worth checking, including nearby airports and typical fare ranges. Don't invent live prices."

ChatGPT gave me a list of potential deals.

It also showed some of its top picks, including San Juan and Barcelona.

As I continued scrolling, ChatGPT eventually showed me a link to Google Flights Explore, one of my absolute favorite tools for finding flight deals. As you can see, this prompt pulls up a Google Flights search for some cheap trips from New York City-area airports to places nearby and, if you scroll the map, far away, too. I had to narrow the search a bit for just trips in January, but there were a ton of options.

You may be asking yourself why you need AI if you are going to Google Flights Explore anyway. Great point — I think the idea is that ChatGPT can give you a few ideas tailored to your specific interests and budget.

AI can also help you find savings by flying into cheaper airports or on different travel dates that will save you some cash. You might try Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) instead of San Francisco International Airport (SFO), for example. Or, further afield, maybe flying into Brussels and taking a train instead of flying directly into Paris can save you money.

"I want to fly from New York to Paris in February 2027. What nearby departure and arrival airports should I compare? Suggest flexible travel dates and explain which alternative airports have reasonable ground transportation."

ChatGPT suggested a few alternate airports for me in Europe.

Of course, that doesn't really help without seeing the prices. But it will give you some more ideas; you can then check the live prices at Google Flights. Here's where it gets more interesting, though. When I kept pushing the AI tool to find actual deals, it gave me a list of fares to various cities, including Frankfurt and Amsterdam. And when I prodded it again with the prompt, "Anything cheaper if I fly straight to Paris?", it found a couple of better deals.

Those are great deals. Just be sure they are actually bookable. In this case, I did not find the same deal on the FrenchBee website or on Google Flights, but I did find it on Icelandair via Expedia (where Chat had directed me).

So in this case, AI was able to find me an actual deal to Paris, though I likely could have found that same deal by starting my search on Google Flights and avoiding multiple steps. Still, I'm a bit flabbergasted that AI has gotten good enough to find actual flight deals.

With Black Friday almost here, this could be among the most useful ways to use AI.

Airlines love advertising discounts of 20%, 30% or even 50%, but those promotions sometimes apply only to base fares, select dates or specific routes.

AI can help readers understand the fine print and calculate their actual savings.

"I'm considering this Black Friday airfare sale. Analyze the terms and conditions, including blackout dates, excluded routes, baggage charges, booking deadlines and whether the discount applies to the base fare or total ticket price. Tell me what I should verify before booking. Here are the terms: [paste sale details]."

For example, Cathay Pacific has a Black Friday deal on now for "round-trip savings from the U.S. to Hong Kong and destinations across Asia, Australia and New Zealand, with 15% to 25% off Economy, 15% to 30% off Premium Economy and 10% off Business."

I tried to find a round-trip fare from Seattle to Hong Kong, which quoted me $2,687 for premium economy. I then asked ChatGPT if it was a good deal using the prompts above.

ChatGPT told me that, essentially, that wasn't a great deal. When I pressed it to find me a better deal, it couldn't. However, it did find an additional coupon I could use: "promotion code US26BF115 for the additional $115 discount and potential 3,000 bonus Asia Miles."

So when you read the TPG guide to the best Black Friday and Cyber Monday, be sure to ask ChatGPT if it's really a good deal.

Remember that a 40% discount on the base fare doesn't necessarily translate into 40% off the total ticket price.

Want to know if you should use cash or points to pay for your flights? Of course, TPG has a great points and miles calculator, but AI can help, too.

Black Friday airfare sales sometimes make paying cash a better deal than redeeming points and miles.

Readers can use AI to calculate the value of their points and compare cash fares against award tickets.

"I found a Black Friday round-trip flight for $450. The same flight costs 35,000 airline miles plus $50 in taxes. Calculate the cents-per-mile value and explain the trade-offs between paying cash and redeeming miles. Assume both tickets offer comparable benefits."

In this hypothetical example, the redemption yields about 1.14 cents per mile, before accounting for any miles earned on a paid ticket.

Here is a link to TPG's latest points and miles valuations, so you can do your own math, too.

As an illustration, I found a round-trip flight on American Airlines from New York City to Madrid in February for $670. Similar flights cost 60,000 plus $52.09 when booked with miles. I asked ChatGPT if it was a good deal. As you can see, based on TPG valuations, ChatGPT tells me to use cash, not miles.

I've found ChatGPT to be extremely useful in telling me whether to spend cash, miles or points on things like hotels and flights.

Related:10 of our favorite travel hacks from very frequent flyers

Despite my best efforts, AI was not able to find me actual deals for specific flights in most cases. AI still works best as a complement to established flight-search tools, not as a replacement.

Here's an example of a search I tried using Claude's AI. While Black Friday hadn't started yet, it had trouble finding any great deals and didn't show anything in real time.

Of course, I've mentioned Google Flights multiple times, as it's likely your best way to find those flight deals.

Another tool that TPG loves is Points Path. Download it to layer on top of Google Flights to flag good deals on points. Points Path can also send you alerts on good award deals.

For the best results, use award search tools like Seats.aero, Roame.travel or Point.me, alongside AI. You can search for business-class availability and even set alerts to be emailed when the award you are looking for opens.

Related: These new tools will track your flights and get you refunds if the price drops

I track my flights with two other new tools. PAiback has given me back $148 this year alone. I've also been experimenting with Junova. Both companies will monitor cash prices and get you refunds if the price drops, charging you a commission on the money saved.

New users at Junova get a $25 credit when signing up through the TPG referral link (so you get a $25 credit — then when you pay the 20% commission, it comes out of your $25 "bank"). We also like Autopilot.

The point of all this is that, in my experience, AI can't yet find good flight or points deals, though I will keep playing with it. My next move is to try to integrate it with one of my flight deal search companies, but we are not there just yet.

As previously mentioned, there is a lot AI still can't do perfectly. Remember that AI can hallucinate fares, routes, promotions and availability. In most cases, AI chatbots have access to live airline pricing; AI tools may present outdated prices or expired deals. AI-generated fare comparisons may also forget taxes, fees or baggage charges. Finally, even if AI finds you a great trip, the itinerary may disappear before you can book it.

And remember, points and miles deals are still very elusive even with the power of artificial intelligence.

As Potter from Thrifty Traveler told me, "In an age when airlines are getting stingier with award space — and there are more savvy travelers redeeming points than ever before — those great award deals are increasingly dynamic, hinging on new routes or airline capacity changes that can appear and vanish within not just hours but minutes."

In other words, AI won't be able to grab you those incredible deals like companies like Thrifty Traveler can.

Always confirm the final price, itinerary and fare rules before purchasing.

As someone who spends a good chunk of every day searching for flight deals, I've been pleasantly surprised by how far artificial intelligence has come. While I'm not ready to give up my favorite flight search tools, AI has earned a place in my travel-planning arsenal.

Whether you're shopping for Black Friday, Cyber Monday or Travel Tuesday deals, AI can help you think outside the box, identify cheaper destinations and alternative airports, decipher complicated sale terms, and determine whether you're better off paying cash or redeeming points and miles.

Just don't take everything AI tells you at face value. I've encountered plenty of fares that I couldn't actually book, and AI still has a long way to go when it comes to finding award availability.

For now, the sweet spot is combining AI with tried-and-true tools like Google Flights, Points Path and flight deal-alert services. And, as always, flexibility remains your greatest asset when looking for cheap flights.

AI may not be the ultimate travel deal finder just yet, but it could help you become a smarter shopper — and save you some serious cash or miles in the process.
