If you have the (see rates and fees), you may have wondered whether it's worth upgrading to the (see rates and fees).

The Quest comes with a higher $350 annual fee, compared to the Explorer's $150 annual fee ($0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150). But it also offers additional perks, including two free checked bags, $200 in annual United TravelBank cash and a head start toward United elite status.

As a Quest cardholder myself, I think the card can be well worth its annual fee; however, there are a few things I'd consider before upgrading.

Here are five reasons you might want to make the switch — and a few things to consider before you do.

Before deciding whether to upgrade, it helps to see how the two cards stack up. Here's a side-by-side comparison of their key benefits.

Related: Which United credit card is right for you? Comparing the Explorer, Quest, Club and Business cards

If you regularly check bags when flying United, you likely already appreciate the 's complimentary first checked bag for you and a companion on the same reservation.

The takes that benefit a step further, offering both your first and second checked bags free for you and a companion on eligible United-operated flights.

It might not sound like much, but it can lead to substantial savings if you regularly travel with multiple bags.

For example, United's second checked bag can cost up to $60 each way on domestic flights. If you and a companion each check two bags on a round-trip flight, the Quest could save you up to $240 in second-bag fees compared to the Explorer.

That's already more than the $200 difference between the cards' ongoing annual fees.

As a Quest cardholder, I've gotten substantial value from this benefit, since I frequently travel with checked bags. Of course, if you rarely check more than one bag, the Explorer's baggage benefit may be all you need.

Keep in mind that to receive the complimentary checked bag benefits, you generally must include your MileagePlus number in the reservation and purchase your tickets with your eligible United card.

Related: Who should (and shouldn’t) get the United Quest Card?

Sure, the might cost $200 more per year than the after the first cardholder year, but there's one perk that can help make up that difference in one fell swoop: the $200 annual United TravelBank benefit.

Quest cardholders automatically receive $200 in United TravelBank cash after account opening and each year on their account anniversary. These funds can be used toward future eligible flights operated by United or United Express.

Meanwhile, Explorer cardholders can earn $100 in United TravelBank cash after spending $10,000 on purchases in a calendar year.

If you regularly book United flights, the Quest's $200 TravelBank benefit should be relatively easy to use. And if you value the full $200, it effectively brings the card's $350 annual fee down to $150 before factoring in any other benefits.

I've personally found this to be one of the most straightforward Quest benefits to maximize. Since I fly United regularly, I typically put my TravelBank cash toward flights when fares are on the higher side, such as cross-country trips from my home base in San Francisco to Washington, D.C., where I have family.

If you know you'll spend at least $200 on eligible United flights each year, this benefit alone could make a strong case for upgrading to the Quest, especially if you aren't currently earning the Explorer's TravelBank benefit.

If you regularly purchase United flights, upgrading to the Quest could help you earn more MileagePlus miles.

The United Quest earns 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights, compared to 9 total miles per dollar spent with the Explorer. These totals include the 6 miles per dollar spent that general MileagePlus members earn on eligible fares, plus 4 miles per dollar spent from the Quest or 3 miles per dollar from the Explorer.

The Quest also earns 4 miles per dollar spent on other eligible United purchases, compared to 3 miles per dollar spent with the Explorer (mileage earning rates differ for Basic Economy or base-option tickets).

That means you'd earn an additional mile per dollar on eligible United spending by upgrading.

For example, if you spend $3,000 on eligible United purchases in a year, you'd earn 3,000 more miles with the Quest than with the Explorer.

While earning more miles is always nice, I wouldn't recommend upgrading solely for this difference. Unless you're spending a substantial amount with United, the additional miles probably won't justify the $200 difference in ongoing annual fees.

But they're a nice bonus if you're already considering the Quest for its other benefits.

If you're trying to earn United Premier status, the Quest offers a couple of advantages over the Explorer.

Both cards earn 1 Premier qualifying point (PQP) for every $20 spent on purchases. However, the Explorer caps these earnings at 1,000 PQP per calendar year, while the Quest allows you to earn up to 18,000 PQP annually through card spending.

The Quest also provides an annual bonus of 1,000 PQP, awarded within six to eight weeks after Feb. 1 each year. To qualify, your account must be open as of Dec. 31 of the previous year and remain open when the points are awarded.

The annual bonus provides a head start toward Premier status without a spending requirement.

As a United Premier Silver member, I've found the Quest's PQP benefits helpful in working toward maintaining my status.

That said, I wouldn't necessarily recommend putting large amounts of everyday spending on the Quest solely to earn PQP. Depending on your goals, you may get more value from using a card that earns transferable rewards.

Both the Explorer and Quest offer statement credits for purchases like ride-hailing services (activation required), Instacart orders and hotel stays. But the Quest offers higher potential savings in several categories.

For example, the Quest provides up to $100 annually in ride-hailing credits and up to $180 in Instacart credits, compared to $60 and $120, respectively, with the Explorer. Both cards' Instacart benefits are currently scheduled to end Dec. 31, 2027.

The Quest also offers up to $150 in annual credits for eligible Renowned Hotels and Resorts stays, up to $80 in United TravelBank cash for qualifying Avis or Budget rentals and up to $150 in annual JSX statement credits.

The Explorer offers similar credits for hotel stays, rental cars and JSX flights, but with lower annual allowances.

I've received some value from Quest's Instacart credit, and while it's nice to save a little on an online grocery order each month, it's not a perk that significantly affects how I value the card.

These credits could help justify the Quest's additional $200 in annual fees if you'll actually use them. Otherwise, I wouldn't give them too much weight in your decision, especially since some have specific booking requirements.

While the offers several advantages over the , upgrading won't make sense for everyone.

If you rarely check a second bag, don't fly United frequently enough to use the $200 annual TravelBank cash or aren't working toward Premier status, the Explorer may offer everything you need at a lower annual fee.

Both cards also share several benefits, including priority boarding, no foreign transaction fees and a credit of up to $120 for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus every four years.

Before upgrading, I'd also consider whether applying for the Quest as a new card makes more sense, since you generally won't receive a welcome offer through a product change.

New cardholders can currently earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQP: 500 PQP after their first purchase, 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening and an additional 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

However, if you're over Chase's 5/24 limit, you may not be eligible to open a new Chase card. In that case, upgrading could be worth considering if the Quest's benefits are a good fit for you.

Depending on your travel habits, it might also make sense to hold both cards. TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak is considering this strategy. She has the United Explorer and appreciates it for its lounge access, but believes she can also get substantial value from the Quest's various United perks.

If you're ready to upgrade from the to the , you'll need to call the number on the back of your credit card. Explain to the representative that you want to upgrade your card to the Quest Card.

Be clear with the agent on the phone that you want to change to the new card to ensure that Chase doesn't process a new card application or close your current card by mistake.

You should be able to continue using your current card until the new one arrives in the mail.

Related: The ultimate guide to credit card upgrades

The is a solid option for occasional United flyers, while the offers additional benefits that can make its higher annual fee worthwhile for frequent travelers.

If you regularly check bags, can use the annual TravelBank cash and value the Quest's other perks, upgrading could make sense. Otherwise, you may be better off sticking with the Explorer.

#6046. Airbus A380 Fuel Burn: How 4 Engines Shape The Superjumbo’s Economics

This October, the Federal Aviation Administration sent a harsh reminder to Airbus A380-800 operators about the cost of four-engine complexity. After an uncontained high-pressure turbine seal failure caused an engine shutdown and an aborted takeoff, the FAA directed the Engine Alliance GP7200 turbofans, which power many of the superjumbos, to be recalled from service for overhaul. Replacing each sub-assembly costs up to $528,150 per engine, demonstrating how four large powerplants compound mechanical difficulties and high hourly fuel costs.

Emirates refuses to treat the double-decker as an operational liability. During its financial year ended in March, the Dubai carrier posted a record $6.2 billion pretax profit and bought out 29 leased A380-800s outright to keep them flying into the 2040s. The airline's leadership openly acknowledged that the superjumbo was the most profitable asset in its whole fleet, wagering billions on multi-class cabin repairs while almost all other international operators scrapped the type.

Because four-engine aircraft consume almost twice as much fuel per hour as a contemporary twinjet and require twice as many shop visits when external maintenance facilities stop, most airline planners steer clear of these aircraft. Emirates packs high-paying fliers into slot-choked international airports where additional daily flights are not feasible, turning an out-of-production giant into its top earner nonetheless.

An Airbus A350-1000 consumes 1,823 gallons (6,900 liters) of jet fuel per hour, whereas four Rolls-Royce Trent 900 or GP7200 turbofans consume about 4,600 gallons (17,413 liters). By cramming up to 600 passengers into slot-rationed hubs like London Heathrow and New York-JFK, Emirates reverses that fuel penalty. At slot-capped airports where Emirates cannot get a second takeoff slot, a single 85%-full A380 carries nearly twice as many high-fare passengers as one 787-9, easily paying for the extra fuel.

While small subfleets decimated rivals in Europe, Dubai's fleet size made it viable. Clark said in November 2019, according to Airline Ratings:

"The A380 was a misfit for Air France. They never scaled, they only have ten aircraft. Yes, we faced the same teething problems, but we dealt with them because we were scaled enough to deal with it. If you've got a sub fleet of 10 it's a bloody nightmare and the costs go through the roof."

Running over a hundred quadjets in-house spreads fixed tooling and spare-engine costs over a large number of daily flying hours. Nonetheless, four engines penalize timetables whenever external repair shops fail. By October, 24 Emirates superjumbos had been parked and seven stored due to engine overhauls, while 84 had flown, exposing an older rift within Dubai's dual-engine sourcing policy that helped doom the assembly line.

Emirates powered its first 90 Airbus A380-800s with GP7200 engines before stunning manufacturers in April 2015 with a $9.2 billion switch to Rolls-Royce Trent 900 turbofans for its final 50 jets. Fine desert sand around Dubai quickly accelerated fan blade wear, delaying deliveries by months and sparking years of haggling that forced Emirates to slash 39 superjumbo orders in February 2019, leaving Airbus CEO Tom Enders without enough backlog to sustain production.

Enders shut down the Toulouse assembly line because selling low volumes below production cost made no financial sense, commenting to NPR: "If you have a product that nobody wants anymore, or you can only sell only below production cost, you have to stop it, as painful as it is." Even so, Clark still campaigns for a modernized A380neo, arguing that next-generation engines and composite wings would cut hourly fuel burn from 26,455 pounds (12 metric tons) to 19,842 pounds (9 metric tons).

Airbus declined until commitments reached about 250 aircraft, despite Clark's insistence that Emirates purchase at least 100 modified superjumbos to enable ultra-long-haul flights from Dubai to Santiago and São Paulo. As MigFlug covered, Clark went on the record, saying: "I'm telling you, we would purchase them if you cross-fertilized A350 or 787 technology into a new A380, which would result in a 25% reduction in operating expenses. A minimum (order) of one hundred is required."

How carriers around the world are filling the jumbo-sized void left by an icon of aviation.

Four engines used to be an airline's best insurance policy over open water, but modern reliability turned that extra hardware into dead weight. Quadjets lost their ocean monopoly overnight when regulators allowed twinjets, such as the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 777-300ER, to fly for six hours on a single engine. On almost all long-haul routes, newer twin-engine widebodies also reduce fuel consumption per seat by 25% to 30%, rendering four-engine aircraft obsolete.

Maintaining four intricate turbofans increases mechanical wear on additional turbine blades and fuel pumps, resulting in maintenance expenditures for the Airbus A380-800 exceeding $6,000 per hour and overall operating expenses of $30,000 per flight hour or more. The FAA's October directive regarding Engine Alliance GP7200 engines demonstrated the high expense of those additional parts. The agency warned in the Federal Register:

"Although the root cause is still under investigation, HPT interstage mid-seal clocking has been identified as a contributing factor for the failure... The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in an engine fire and damage to the airplane."

Doubling the engine count also increases a fleet's vulnerability to rare, catastrophic manufacturing flaws. In November 2010, Qantas Flight 32 experienced a massive Rolls-Royce Trent 900 explosion over Indonesia after a fractured pipe wall thinner than 0.02 inches (0.5 mm) shattered a turbine disk and severed 650 wing wires. Seven years later, Air France Flight 66 lost an outboard GP7200 fan hub over Greenland at 37,000 feet (11,278 meters) because microscopic strain cracked the forged titanium.

The compromise on the factory floor that stopped the 747's 21st Century evolution.

Due to weight and simple aerodynamics, two large engines outperform four smaller ones. Compared to the Airbus A380-800's four smaller GP7200 or Rolls-Royce Trent 900 pods, modern twinjets like the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 777-9 have enormous composite fans beneath each wing that drive massive columns of slower air with far less drag. Additionally, the wing loses thousands of pounds of structural weight and friction when two engine housings and pylons are cut.

Airbus built 25% of the superjumbo from lightweight composites and cutting-edge metals to counteract the weight penalty of four engines. Engineers constructed aviation's first carbon-composite center wing box, saving 3,307 pounds (1.5 metric tons), and topped the fuselage with GLARE aluminum-glass laminates to stop fatigue cracks. Underneath, dropped-hinge wing flaps sealed trailing-edge gaps, so air flowed smoothly across the massive 261.8-foot (79.8-meter) wingspan during high-altitude cruise.

116-inch (2.96-meter) fan; 14,811 pounds (6,718 kg) dry

74,735 to 80,290 pounds of thrust (332.4 to 357.1 kN); 8.7:1 bypass; 36.92:1 pressure ratio

Pairs nine-stage GE90 core with hollow titanium fan

Higher core pressure cuts per-seat fuel burn 25% to 30%

Massive twin fan diameters replace two extra engine pods

Blending stiff carbon ribs with high-strength aluminum wing skins still triggered a costly cracking crisis in 2012. Tiny assembly gaps stressed internal wing brackets until they split, forcing expensive fleetwide repairs. Airbus executive Richard Carcaillet explained to AIN Online: "The solution involves replacing the current wing rib feet—L-shaped brackets that attach the wing ribs to the skins made with the comparatively new, Alcan 7449 aluminum alloy—with rib feet made from slightly heavier, 7010 aluminum used in the A330."

The outlandish atomic flying colossus designed to be the ultimate Cold War lightning carrier.

Airbus absorbed over $330 million in wing-crack repairs across a $25 billion program that never broke even. Enders admitted to Bloomberg in July 2012: "Airbus thought it understood the properties of the A380 wing materials and the interface between carbon fiber and metal, but found out the wrong way we didn't know everything. It has cost the company a great deal of money and [harmed our] reputation." Yet Emirates turned that troubled airframe into an unmatched moneymaker.

Twin decks give Emirates 5,920 square feet (550 square meters) of floor space, letting Dubai install onboard bars, showers, and upstairs premium economy cabins no twinjet could spare. Clark explained to the Points Guy in 2019: "Why was it that it was Emirates, who took it after Singapore Airlines, that it lit up the planet in terms of showers and bars and big TV screens? We did it for a very well-calculated reason... we had taken a huge risk and huge investment."

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Cash-rich and parts-hungry, Emirates invested $5 billion in cabin refits, bought out 29 leased superjumbos, and agreed in November to acquire six more from Qatar's Lesha Bank. Teardown math drives that buying spree: used A380-800s trade cheaply, while one fresh landing gear set or four serviceable engines cost nearly as much as a complete plane. Dubai is cannibalizing its earliest retired frames for spares as Airbus factory support winds down.

#6045. Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:

The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

#6044. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”

Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG

Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

#6041. JetBlue Cancels 11 International Routes: See Full List Now

JetBlue is the USA's fourth-largest airline for international service. In November 2026, for example, the carrier has 2,723 departures beyond the US border, equivalent to 91 daily flights. Compared to last November, activity has fallen by 9%.

The international arena is a relatively large part of JetBlue's total offering. In the same month, 20% of services are international, more than double the rate for the US's ten largest operators. However, multiple cuts, including those mentioned in this article, have reduced JetBlue's share from 23% last November.

It is common to compare how things have changed between two periods of time, such as different months, quarters, half years, or years. Cirium Diio data was used to see which international routes JetBlue operated in November 2025 but which do not exist in November 2026.

11 links were identified, most of which existed from New York JFK — historically the airline's most-served airport — and Newark. While they could simply have become seasonal or, at least, focused more on the peak periods, that is not the case. They have all been removed. Moreover, as disclosed recently, JetBlue has pulled out of Antigua, Bonaire, Belize City, and Tulum entirely.

Routes Served Last November But Not This November

Following heavy losses, JetBlue removed many underperforming or less significant international routes network-wise as a part of its JetForward restructuring. Compared to last November, such flights from New York JFK have fallen by a considerable 24%, while Boston (a much smaller station for such activity) is down by 16%. Newark has decreased by 68%, with only one route now served, while Orlando is 29% lower.

Despite the reductions, New York JFK remains JetBlue's number one airport for service beyond the US border. It has 42% of the departures in November, reduced from half 12 months ago. What has really changed is the rise of Fort Lauderdale, at which the carrier is increasingly focusing (internationally and domestically), partly because of the exit of Spirit Airlines.

International flights from the South Florida airport are up 63%, with Fort Lauderdale now accounting for 29% of JetBlue's total, 13 points more than 12 months ago. It is developing a mini-hub, of sorts, between the US and the Caribbean and Latin America. Excluding US territories, 18 international routes are available in November, with more coming in 2027.

One of the two new routes seems to be doing particularly badly, with big changes coming. Find out more here!

Several of the 11 routes were pulled after relatively little time, which is often the case, even without a program like JetForward. If the initial performance is not sufficiently good relative to expectations, and the network contribution is not important enough, it is sensible to redeploy the expensive aircraft to where they may perform better.

New York JFK to San Pedro Sula flights lasted for less than a year, influenced by a very low load factor of just 68.1%. The carrier decided to consolidate on its Fort Lauderdale service, which began in November 2025, with that route's traffic figures rising as a result.

Initial data from the US Department of Transportation demonstrates this. Between November 2025 and the following April, when JFK flights still existed, Fort Lauderdale's average load factor was 62.5%. Ouch. But from May 2026 to August 2026 (as far as the data currently extends), it jumped to 90.1%. Given that more and more lower-yielding transit traffic is probably carried now, yields may have fallen.

#6040. Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:

The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:

Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM

The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around.

While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

#6039. Delta Air Lines Launches 15 New International Routes: See Full List Now

As the northern aviation winter season is here, airlines are increasingly finalizing their plans for next summer. Initial information for Q3 2027 (July-September) shows that Delta Air Lines is planning 258 daily international departures in the all-important period (double for total movements).

The SkyTeam member's offering is currently expected to be 6% higher than for Q3 2026, with 14 daily departures added. It will be the seventh-highest volume on record for that quarter. However, it is subject to change, as Delta firms up its plan. Still, 15 new and returning routes will help, some of which will be operating in the third quarter of 2027, having not done so in 2026.

For this article, Delta's international network in Q3 2026 was compared to what is planned for Q3 2027 using Cirium Diio data. 15 international routes were identified, eight of which are long-haul. As all markets have already been officially announced, this article simply summarizes what is happening and provides some additional context.

Only routes that have already been disclosed and are scheduled are included. As such, any upcoming new link from Seattle, expected to be revealed on December 2, is excluded. While flights to Singapore have been increasingly speculated, this is not entirely certain. Even so, it is unclear when, precisely, they'd begin.

Medium & Long-Haul Routes: Didn't Operate In Q3 2026 But Will In Q3 2027

A brand-new market. The launch was postponed for half a year. Suggestions that this will be delayed to the second half of 2027

A brand-new market. It'll connect the Texas capital with the hugely important European SkyTeam hub. It'll be Delta's only long-haul route from Austin. Interestingly, flights will arrive in Texas at 4:52 PM and leave at 3:15 PM. Is another route coming?!

Previously served in 2021. Replaces Detroit-Reykjavík Keflavík, which Delta last served in 2026. Delta ended that route shortly after Icelandair did. Boston-Reykjavík Keflavík will be the airline's new shortest route to Europe

A brand-new market. Venice is the largest unserved European city from Boston

A brand-new market. The capital of Greece is the #1 unserved European market from Detroit

New for Delta, but Northwest flew via Tokyo Narita until 2009 using the 747-400. Delta flew to the Philippines via Narita until 2020, just not beginning/ending in Los Angeles

Inherited from Northwest. Delta previously operated until 2020

None of the following links are brand-new, which is perhaps not surprising. None of them are new to Delta's map in 2026, although two links were inaugurated in December 2025. They include Austin to Los Cabos, with Delta joining American (albeit only January, March, and April 2027) and Southwest. In Q3 2027, Delta's offering contributes to that market having a record number of flights.

Many of the entries are markets that Delta already serves. They are simply included because flights did not operate in Q3 2026 but are scheduled to do so in the same quarter next year. In many ways, this is a vote of confidence for a route. Obviously, the reverse (a shorter operating period with fewer flights and less capacity) may indicate problems. Just ask Southwest about one of its links to Alaska.

Short-Haul Routes: Didn't Operate In Q3 2026 But Will In Q3 2027

Route operated between December 2025 and April 2026. It didn't run in Q3 last year, but will now do so

New for Delta. Originally, flights began in December 2025 and existed until April 2026. They'll resume next month and operate year-round

Weekly to daily A321ceo, 737-800, 737-900ER

Served by Delta for years (and Northwest before that). Operated until May 2026, but will now run through July, just making Q3

On Delta's map until 2005 and from 2017. In 2026, flights existed until June. They'll return in November and operate year-round

Part of the airline's network from 2007-2008 and 2014-2018. Third time's a charm?

Delta previously served this route in 2007 and 2013-2014. Just replaced flights from New York JFK. First time that two operators have existed concurrently from LaGuardia to Bermuda

Served by Delta since 2015. In 2026, flights operated until June and returned in November. In 2027, they'll run year-round

One of the two new routes seems to be doing particularly badly, with big changes coming. Find out more here!

For obvious reasons, Delta's total flights on the aging, fuel-inefficient, maintenance-heavy, but clearly characterful Boeing 757 have fallen dramatically in recent years. Only 8,455 movements are scheduled on the 757-200 and 757-300 in Q3 2027, down by 60% compared to Q3 2026. Retirements have contributed to this reduction, while nine A321neos were delivered in September and October 2026 alone.

The decrease is due to the domestic market (-67% year-over-year). In contrast, 30% more international 757 flights are planned between next July and September, although this is still far below historic levels. This is not because of the relaunch of service from Boston to Iceland after a five-year absence, as that is just replacing the 757 link from Detroit to the nation. In contrast, Q3 flights from Los Angeles to Mexico City do contribute, although this is only one part of the picture.

#6038. Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card

Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

The card also has no extra cost to add authorized users, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:

Personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

Southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

Preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

The Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

On your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

If you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

Many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

That said, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

First, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:

The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:

I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

If you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

If you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. Southwest credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification in 2027, and this card’s 90,000-point welcome offer can get you a good chunk of the way there.

#6035. Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself…

Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

Getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

Ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

#6034. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

“I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

“I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

“Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”

Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

“I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”

Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”

“We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

“That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

“There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”

It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

“My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

“The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”

That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

“I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

#6033. American Airlines’ Lag Linked To Flyers Unphased By Delta & United’s High Fares, Analyst Says

American Airlines is struggling to match the financial performance of its two biggest domestic rivals, and passengers' willingness to pay higher fares to fly Delta Air Lines and United Airlines may be a major factor. According to Dan McKenzie, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners, both carriers command considerably higher fares than American on comparable flights, according to The New York Times.

McKenzie estimates that American needs approximately $4.5 billion in additional annual revenue to match its competitors' profit margins. With surging jet fuel costs pressuring airline profitability, the ability to command higher fares without significantly compromising demand has become increasingly important. American's latest disappointing financial results illustrate the scale of that challenge.

McKenzie's analysis found that Delta commands fares that are 12% above the industry average on similar flights, compared with 9% at United and just 3% at American. To illustrate, on a flight with an industry-average fare of $500, Delta could command $560 and United $545 without impacting demand, compared with $515 at American. Across millions of passengers, those differences quickly accumulate.

Interestingly, American achieved the strongest passenger yield growth of the three carriers during the third quarter of 2026. However, an analysis of their respective financial results reveals that American also experienced the largest decline in load factor. Consequently, its passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) increased more slowly than at either Delta or United.

While American's faster capacity growth also contributed to its declining load factor, the results partly reflect a deliberate commercial strategy. The airline historically prioritized filling its aircraft, but is increasingly focused on improving yields. Speaking during American's third-quarter earnings call, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper explained the trade-off.

"We have prioritized yield over load factor, proactively securing meaningfully higher yields in exchange for slightly lower loads."

Delta and United have spent years differentiating their onboard products, recognizing the growing demand for premium travel. That strategy is delivering substantial financial returns. In the third quarter, United's premium and loyalty revenues both rose 17% year over year. Meanwhile, Delta's premium ticket revenue actually surpassed main cabin ticket revenue, with the latter accounting for less than 40% of its adjusted operating revenue.

Nowhere is this more evident than with corporate travelers, whose purchasing decisions are often influenced more by schedule convenience, operational reliability, and loyalty benefits than by fares. Delta topped the Business Travel News' 2026 Airline Survey for the 16th consecutive year, outperforming its competitors in eight of the 11 categories assessed. Despite substantial improvements, American remained the lowest-ranked qualifying airline.

Network composition is another important differentiator. Delta and United have greater exposure to affluent coastal markets, with both offering nearly twice as many departing seats from the most affluent, New York, as American. This also underscores the commercial significance of American's intensifying battle with United at Chicago O'Hare, where higher frequency and connectivity could help it secure more lucrative corporate travel contracts.

American Airlines is abandoning its legal challenge over Chicago's gate redistribution, but its battle with United is far from over.

American is pursuing a comprehensive transformation of its passenger experience, reversing several previous management decisions. These include reintroducing narrowbody seatback screens and substantially expanding premium seating. However, several of its most significant product enhancements will take years to implement across the fleet, delaying their full commercial impact.

Increase from 25% to approximately 40% of seats

800+ narrowbodies; new deliveries from 2028

1,000+ mainline aircraft; rollout from 2027

Boeing 787-9s, Airbus A321XLRs and 777 retrofits

All 20 aircraft by 2027; premium seating increasing from 38% to 44%

There are encouraging signs that American's strategy is gaining traction. Its premium revenue increased 22.9% year-on-year in the third quarter, while managed corporate revenue increased 27.6%, marking its sixth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. American's corporate travel satisfaction score has also improved this year, suggesting its efforts to rebuild relationships are paying dividends.

However, American is pursuing a moving target. While it prepares to begin installing Starlink in 2027, United already offers the service on more than half of its daily flights. And while Delta offers its personalized Delta Sync seatback entertainment experience on more than 900 aircraft, American will only begin its seatback screen rollout from 2028. So, as its rivals continue to reinvest profits in product differentiation, American's ultimate challenge will be persuading passengers that its flights are equally worth paying more for.

#6032. New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”

The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:

The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy

While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉

As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

#6031. BermudAir Adding Flights All Over The Place: I Don’t Know What’s Going On

BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

Several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:

On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:

Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed…

I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:

I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:

What’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know…

It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”

What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?
