#6030. At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

“We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

“I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

“I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”

Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

#KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”

Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

#INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

New leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

#6029. The Most Frequent JetBlue Airbus A320 Routes In 2026

JetBlue’s busiest Airbus A320 route in 2026 is not a transcontinental link between two major business centers. According to Cirium, it is Orlando–San Juan, a leisure-heavy connection that recorded 3,562 flights in both directions in the supplied flight-tracking dataset. More revealing still, all 11 busiest A320 city pairs touch Florida, putting the airline’s New York roots alongside a network heavily concentrated in the Sunshine State.

That pattern raises a question a route ranking alone cannot answer: is JetBlue deliberately building a deeper Florida operation, or taking advantage of a gap left by the defunct Spirit Airlines while trying to improve its financial performance? The answer involves Orlando’s reach, Fort Lauderdale’s rapid expansion, the difference between counting flights and measuring capacity, and the A320’s role as JetBlue reshapes its fleet.

Orlando–San Juan sits at the center of the pattern because it combines frequency with meaningful distance. JetBlue operated 1,782 flights from Orlando International Airport (MCO) to Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU), offering 286,596 seats, and another 1,780 in the opposite direction, offering 286,380. Together, that is 3,562 flights and 572,976 seats across an average sector length of 1,189 miles (1,914 km).

The route generated approximately 681.3 million available seat miles (ASMs), or around 1.1 billion available seat kilometers. ASMs multiply the seats offered by the distance flown; they measure capacity, not passengers carried. The near-identical totals in each direction also suggest demand is relatively balanced rather than dominated by one-way seasonal traffic.

The route links two of the five cities where JetBlue described itself as a leading carrier in its January 2026 announcement: Orlando and San Juan. Leisure travelers and people visiting friends and relatives give the route more than one source of demand, helping support frequency without relying on traditional corporate traffic. But the lead over Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia is only 212 flights, or about 6%. Why, then, is Fort Lauderdale becoming such a consequential part of the airline’s plans?

Fort Lauderdale’s importance is rooted in JetBlue’s history as well as its current expansion. The airline’s first revenue flight in February 2000 connected New York-JFK with Fort Lauderdale. More than 25 years later, Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia remains one of its busiest A320 corridors, with 3,350 combined flights and 542,688 seats across 1,076 miles (1,732 km). Fort Lauderdale–San Juan follows with 3,280 flights and 531,288 seats over 1,046 miles (1,683 km).

The immediate catalyst is Spirit Airlines’ collapse. JetBlue moved to fill part of the gap and said it intended to reach around 150 daily departures from Fort Lauderdale by year-end. Its July announcement put summer departures near 130, more than 75% above 2025 levels, while adding service to destinations including Baltimore, Charlotte, Cleveland, Nashville, Detroit, Houston, Chicago and Ponce. CBS Miami reported on the expansion as an effort to fill gaps left by Spirit.

The plan is about more than replacing individual routes. As documented by Aviation Week, JetBlue has discussed as many as 370 connecting itineraries through Fort Lauderdale, giving the airport a larger role in the network. The fixed flight dataset may under-represent recently launched services, so the current route mix is a snapshot rather than a final picture of the expansion. The leading routes nevertheless show how Florida connects to JetBlue’s wider network:

JetBlue is doubling down at FLL just as Spirit Airlines is forced to pull back.

Orlando’s footprint is broader than the leading San Juan route suggests. Across the six city pairs in the 11-route group that cross Orlando, the airport accounts for 14,507 flights. Fort Lauderdale accounts for 10,981 across four pairs, while West Palm Beach contributes another 2,156 through its Westchester service. JetBlue’s Florida presence is therefore spread across three airports rather than resting on one dominant base.

Orlando represents about 52% of the flights in the 11-route group. Fort Lauderdale’s role is different: it combines New York services with Caribbean flying and a fast-growing list of new destinations. New York remains the other half of the pattern, with seven of the 11 city pairs connecting a New York-area airport — JFK, LaGuardia, Newark, or Westchester — with Florida. Boston and San Juan account for two pairs each.

The New York side is changing too. JFK’s New Terminal One has slipped to early 2027, while Terminal 6 is expected to host JetBlue, according to Simple Flying reporting. With service spread across four New York-area airports, the airline must balance geographic coverage against overlapping capacity. And flight totals alone cannot show which routes contribute most to the network’s capacity: how does the picture change when distance is included?

A flight count treats every departure equally, whether it covers 944 miles (1,519 km) or 1,237 miles (1,991 km). ASMs provide another perspective by multiplying seats offered by distance flown. Orlando–San Juan remains the largest route on this measure, at approximately 681.3 million ASMs. Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia follows with 583.9 million, while Fort Lauderdale–San Juan generates about 555.7 million.

The movement further down the network is more revealing. Fort Lauderdale–Boston recorded 2,151 flights over an average distance of 1,237 miles (1,991 km), producing about 430.7 million ASMs. Orlando–Boston operated more flights, at 2,222, but its shorter 1,121-mile (1,804-km) sector generated approximately 398.9 million ASMs. Fort Lauderdale–Boston therefore contributes more capacity despite operating fewer flights.

JetBlue’s third-quarter 2026 results underline why capacity and profitability must be considered separately. The airline reported an 18.4% increase in revenue per available seat mile (RASM), while average fuel reached $3.91 per gallon, 57% higher year over year. Its third-quarter results release also said BlueFirst, its new domestic first-class product, would begin operating on Boston–Fort Lauderdale on December 8. That longer route gains importance when capacity is measured in seat-miles, and the premium product suggests JetBlue sees an opportunity to earn more from at least some of its Florida services. What does the A320 cabin itself reveal about how the airline matches capacity to demand?

Discover the airline that consistently delivers the widest standard economy seats today, offering passengers a genuinely roomy cabin experience.

JetBlue and Simple Flying show two A320 layouts: the Classic configuration with 150 seats and the Restyled version with 162. The supplied flight data offers an indirect way to estimate where each may be used more often, although it cannot identify individual aircraft. Fort Lauderdale–LaGuardia, Fort Lauderdale–San Juan, Fort Lauderdale–Newark, and Westchester–West Palm Beach average close to 162 seats per departure, pointing toward the higher-capacity Restyled aircraft.

Orlando–LaGuardia is different, averaging 158.9 seats per flight. If the two published layouts are the only configurations in the dataset, that average would be consistent with roughly one in four departures using the 150-seat Classic. This remains an inference, not a confirmed aircraft assignment, because aircraft swaps and schedule changes can affect route averages.

The 12-seat difference still matters at scale. Across 3,562 Orlando–San Juan flights, operating the 162-seat aircraft instead of the 150-seat version on every departure would represent as many as 42,744 additional seats. JetBlue continues to market 32 inches (81 centimeters) of economy pitch, but additional seats only improve the economics if they can be sold at fares that cover fuel, labor, and other operating costs. With the A320 accounting for 129 of JetBlue’s 298 aircraft as of September 30, 2026, how might the arrival of more A220s change that equation?

Fort Lauderdale’s expansion is expected to take the airport beyond 150 daily departures this winter. According to Simple Flying, citing Cirium schedule data, Fort Lauderdale is now JetBlue's busiest airport by scheduled departures, ahead of JFK and Boston, with roughly 21,500 winter departures against nearly 13,700 a year earlier. JetBlue’s July announcement included new services to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia, Indianapolis and Columbus, alongside routes launched earlier in the year. A Mint-equipped San Diego service was scheduled for November 19, while Caracas remained without a confirmed start date in the supplied material. Not every new route will use an A320, however.

Mint class requires the A321, and more premium flying from Fort Lauderdale could direct some growth toward larger aircraft rather than simply adding A320 frequencies. Meanwhile, JetBlue’s fleet plan lists seven A220 deliveries in 2027, nine in 2028, 10 in 2029, and two in 2030. The smaller A220 gives the airline another capacity option for markets where demand may not justify an A320, potentially allowing it to reserve larger aircraft for stronger corridors.

The fleet transition is taking place while JetBlue is still working to improve its finances. The supplied analysis cites Air Data News for a third-quarter loss of $257 million and a fall in cash from $1.95 billion at the end of 2025 to $1.26 billion in September; JetBlue is targeting sustained profitability in 2027. Yet the airline also reported that Fort Lauderdale’s RASM increased nearly 15% in the third quarter despite capacity growth of more than 65%. The test is whether that revenue performance can hold as more flights enter the schedule.

If JetBlue keeps adding capacity to established Florida routes, the network may become even more concentrated around Orlando and Fort Lauderdale. If A220 deliveries allow it to open thinner markets while reserving A320s and A321s for stronger corridors, the pattern could diversify. The route data captures a moment of rapid change; the next fleet and schedule decisions will show whether Florida is becoming JetBlue’s lasting growth engine or simply its biggest opportunity in 2026.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6028. LATAM Refused My Refund Within 24 Hours, And The Reason Makes No Sense

Over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked. I called customer service to cancel within the 24-hour cooling-off period, but was refused a refund for the most convoluted and unnecessary reason.

LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline. It’s an airline I look forward to flying with for several reasons. However, this recent booking experience has uncovered a gaping hole in its customer service, which in the air I’ve always found to be excellent.

This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.

The Brazilian site has no issue when entering UK credit card details.

However, the default setting for postcodes (ZIP codes) is numerical-only because, as in the US, Brazil’s postcodes consist only of numbers. In the UK, they’re made up of letters and numbers, so I couldn’t add the postcode that my credit card is registered to.

I tried using only the numbers of my postcode (the one in the example above is random), but the site returned an error, saying it failed to connect to my bank. My guess would be this wouldn’t be a problem for US credit cards, given that ZIP codes consist only of numbers too.

I remember this happening previously, but I never had an issue with a booking that I couldn’t change online.

Ideally, I would have paid with a Brazilian bank account or credit card, but I’m still working through the immigration bureaucracy required to open one.

First of all, I tried to cancel by logging into my LATAM Pass account, but was redirected to the contact center. This is when I realized how much of an obstacle my booking via the UK website would be.

After being put on hold 3 times for what seemed like forever, the agent I spoke with at LATAM’s Brazilian call center told me there was nothing she could do to help me.

She explained the only way I’d get a refund was to call the UK call center, since I’d paid in GBP on the UK website. I called just before the cut-off of the 24-hour cooling-off period, so by then I had exceeded it. I had only left it so close to the cooling-off period because I was researching the trip again the following day and found a better deal; otherwise, I wouldn’t have wanted to cancel.

If I had called sooner and had more time, I could have asked someone in the UK to call for me, as my Brazilian phone number can’t make outgoing international calls. I did top up my UK SIM Card with 20 GBP, but at a charge of 2 GBP per minute, the call disconnected after 10 minutes on hold with no answer.

Irrespective of whether I could have found an easier way to contact the UK call center, I can’t help but feel that my issue should have been resolved there and then over the phone by the Brazilian call center agent. After all, I booked directly through the airline’s website, and then called the airline directly to cancel. It makes no logical sense!

Because of a stupidly convoluted system, I’m stuck with a LATAM ticket that I can no longer cancel, even though I called customer service within the 24-hour cooling-off period.

It’s not the end of the world, as we can still take the flights we’d originally booked, but it’s so frustrating to be put in a situation like this in 2026 because of such an archaic technicality.

I’m still a big fan of LATAM itself, and will continue to fly it, at least until my Platinum status runs out next year.

What’s the most frustrating post-sale customer service experience you’ve had?

These posts are quite odd, seems like all of Daniel's are. Sorry but I will filter his to avoid them. Not sure this has been a good decision

@Daniel--I am a bit confused as to why you couldn't enter your alphanumeric post code in the first place. When I book on international websites and they ask for address information, there is usually a field for country. If I enter United States in the country field before entering the rest of my data, the site usually changes the nature of the post/zip code and state (if there is one) fields such that I am able to enter appropriate information. Were you not able to enter the UK as your country? If you were, it should have allowed you to enter an appropriate UK post code as part of your address. If it didn't, I would say that is LATAM's fault. If the 24 hour refund rule applies, I would say you are entitled to a refund. Of course, I don't work for LATAM. 😃

Hey Daniel! Not sure how long you’ve been living in Brazil, but a very efficieny way to solve these kinds of issues is through a government platform called consumidor.gov. Companies are obligated to answer all complaints filed there in a couple a days or else they pay a hefty fine, and this seems the sort of situtation thats typically addresses through this channel. You have to have a Brazilian CPF number, though, I think, not sure if you have one yet. Hope it helps =)

Hey Daniel! Canadian postal codes also have numbers and letters like in the UK (for example: K1A3R8). This tip works for Canadian credit cards and you can try to see if it works with UK credit cards as well. Whenever you have to type your postal code and the machine (such as self service gas pumps) or website only accepts numbers, type the numbers in your postal code followed by two zeros. So, K1A3R8 becomes 13800. It always works for Canadian credit cards. Try the same with your UK card and it may work. I’m Canadian and Brazilian and this has helped me lots of times to use my Canadian credit card on Brazilian and US websites.

#6027. Orient Express Sailing Yachts Review: Corinthian’s Suites, Dining, Amenities, Service, And More

For the main event of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, Ford and I had the chance to spend four nights on the Corinthian, which is the first ship in Orient Express’ new cruising venture, known as Orient Express Sailing Yachts.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts set sail in the summer of 2026, and with just 54 suites that can accommodate up to 110 guests, it really brings luxury cruising to a new level. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry more broadly, given how competition has been heating up.

I also recently reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, and had a great experience, and reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which is definitely more luxurious, but also has some growing pains. Lastly, I’ve compared all the experiences as well.

While Orient Express Sailing Yachts is the highest priced cruising venture to date, I have to say, the experience really is unbelievably good, and at least you feel like you’re getting an amazing experience. I come into these kinds of trips with a critical eye, and I was just blown away by the ship’s design, the quality of the food and drinks, and the service. To me the ship felt like a step back in time (in terms of its classic elegance), while also being cutting edge modern.

If you can swing this experience, I’d highly recommend it. Okay, enough of an intro, here comes my 8,500-word review (yikes, this is the longest review I’ve ever published of anything).

Orient Express Sailing Yachts charges per suite (rather than per person, based on double occupancy), and you’ll find that journeys typically cost an average of $4,000-6,000 per cabin per night for a base suite. Make no mistake, this is the very top end of the cruise market, and at this point you’re paying safari prices for the experience.

Let me also emphasize that rates go up from there, and Orient Express Sailing Yachts has some of the most insane suites you’ll find at sea, some of which can cost six figures per sailing. Currently, Orient Express offers cruises in Europe in summer, and in the Caribbean in winter, with transatlantic sailings in the spring and fall.

For what it’s worth, you’ll find rate parity regardless of which booking channel you reserve through. So your best bet is to book through a travel advisor affiliated with Accor Preferred, because they can add perks to your journey. The size of the credit depends on the accommodation type booked, plus the length of the journey.

In the interest of full disclosure, Ford was invited on this Orient Express Sailing Yachts journey (due to the amount of volume he books), and I tagged along with him. All opinions expressed are my own, and I plan to review this exactly the same way I reviewed the two previous cruises (which we paid full price for). I haven’t been asked to write anything, and I have no incentive to be anything other than honest. If people are going to drop a ton of money on a luxury cruise, I want to make sure they’re at least getting the best experience possible.

We experienced Orient Express Sailing Yachts in early October 2026, shortly before the ship’s transatlantic sailing. Admittedly it wasn’t the most exciting itinerary, but that’s just what worked out for us in terms of timing, since we wanted to minimize our time away from home, had to schedule it around when family could best be with our kids, etc. Below is the itinerary for the sailing we took.

We were happy with this itinerary, since our primary goal was to see the ship. It definitely wasn’t the most exciting, though, given that we docked at the port in Mahón (rather than tendering), and it also meant we didn’t have a marina day (not that you’d necessarily want that in October, since it’s a bit chillier). But the point is that if you’re traveling more in peak season, you can expect a marina day more consistently.

Historically, cruising has been all about offering an all-inclusive experience. That’s true with Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, but then Four Seasons Yachts countered the trend, by only including breakfast, and then charging extra for lunch, dinner, and drinks (I don’t love this concept, especially given the quality issues they have).

While Orient Express Sailing Yachts might charge a lot, what I really appreciate is how the company has an ultra all-inclusive concept, to an extent that’s even greater than you’ll find on most other cruise lines. Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys include the following:

Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys don’t include the following:

Regarding the Orient Express Sailing Yachts tipping policy, the company states that gratuities are included in the fare — “however, if you wish to offer a tip as an extra gesture of appreciation, it will be warmly received.”

I just have to emphasize that the level of inclusions really impressed me. Seriously, I was served caviar with breakfast, lunch, and dinner at various points (and even cocktails!), and the house champagne is Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 (which retails for around $200 per bottle).

Orient Express Sailing Yachts currently has a single ship, which is named the Corinthian (a second ship is being introduced in 2027, and it’ll be named the Olympian).

The ship entered service in 2026, and is 722 feet (220 meters) long, 82 feet (25 meters) wide, and 26,600 gross tons. With 54 accommodations and a maximum capacity of around 110 guests, there’s a roughly 1.5:1 staff to guest ratio, given that there are around 170 staff onboard. The spaciousness of this ship, and the amount of space allocated to each passenger, really is next level.

The Corinthian also has the title of being the world’s largest sailing yacht, as it has three automated SolidSail rigid sails on tilting carbon masts, to provide wind propulsion, alongside hybrid LNG auxiliary power. It’s just such an elegant and distinctive looking ship, that it can’t help but turn heads. For those curious, it was explained that the sails reduce emissions by around 10%, and no, the ship doesn’t “heel” in the way a smaller sailboat would. Unless you’re looking up, you wouldn’t realize there are even sails.

You can find the full Corinthian deck plan here. As you’d expect for a sail boat, there aren’t quite as many floors as on a traditional cruise ship. Guests can access a total of five floors, between levels three and seven. To briefly cover that:

Near the ship’s entrance, you’ll find a very cool directory of sorts, which shows the floorplan of the ship. You can click any amenity, and then it will light up, so that’s super handy.

The ship has two sets of elevator banks, as well as two sets of staircases, so getting around the ship is really easy. We always used the stairs, since we were typically within a couple of floors of where we needed to be.

As you’d expect, the ease of boarding a ship varies greatly depending on its size, but Orient Express Sailing Yachts really took it to the next level in terms of how seamless it was. We had spent a night at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. Our journey included the transfers, so an Orient Express representative met us at the hotel, and then we were driven to the port.

Getting onboard the ship literally couldn’t have been easier. There were no formalities in the port, but instead, we were escorted straight through security, and then check-in was handled once onboard.

There were no other guests as we boarded, and the staff really went above and beyond — for example, the crew member who escorted us through security and onto the ship insisted on holding an umbrella over our heads, to shade us from the sun.

Our check-in process onboard took all of five minutes, and at that point we were introduced to our butler, Reuben, who escorted us to our suite, and took care of everything from there. I should mention how Reuben was German, so they specifically appointed us a German butler, which I thought was super fun (so we communicated with him exclusively in German).

We didn’t have a stop that involved tendering, but for those situations where you do, it’s an efficient process, given how few guests there are. Our one stop had us docked in port, and there was a nice seating area outside the ship with bottled water, sunscreen, etc. Admittedly a setup like this is more useful when you’re waiting on a tender, rather than just walking directly onto or off the ship.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has 54 suites onboard, spread across over a dozen different categories. The entry level suites here are among the most spacious at sea, while the penthouse suites really take luxury and space to the next level.

Our sailing was rather empty — only 19 of the 54 suites were occupied — and we were upgraded to a higher suite category (I believe they had blocked most of the entry level room categories, as they were doing some minor updates to them ahead of the ship heading to the Caribbean). So let me share my thoughts on that suite first, and then I’ll share some pictures of other suites that I had the opportunity to tour as well.

We stayed in an Appartement Prestige, which is one of the more premium standard suite categories, but below the duplex suites and penthouse suites. These suites are marketed as being an average of 1,119 square feet (104 square meters), so they’re incredibly spacious.

We were assigned suite 518, located on the fifth floor. The hallways on the Corinthian are just stunning, as you can see below. It really feels more like a luxury hotel than a ship, especially in terms of the width of the hallway.

The concept of forgetting that one is on a ship continued inside the suite. The interior felt more to me like a “Palace” hotel in France, than what you’d expect at sea. I can’t even imagine how much money was spent on the interiors, as the quality of the finishes, from the wall treatments to the carpet, as well as the furniture, was just unreal.

Upon entering the suite, there was first a dining area with a table and a chair, as well as a desk with a chair (that chair could also be moved over to the dining table). It’s not often you get this kind of space in a cruise ship suite.

The minibar was also in this area, and was well stocked, with everything being complimentary. This included a Nespresso coffee machine, cocktails, wine, beer, soft drinks, etc. They were also happy to replenish the minibar however you wanted, so there are really no limits.

That entry area then flowed into the living room, which was gorgeous. It had a couch and a coffee table, as well as a hidden TV (which would pop up from in front of the mirror).

Waiting on the dining table was a lovely welcome amenity, consisting of some freshly baked treats, a fruit plate, and a bottle of Veuve Clicquot 2015 Rose. There was also an Orient Express branded journal, along with two Orient Express water bottles, which guests could take home.

Double doors then led into the bedroom, which had a very plush king size bed.

Much like with the bedroom, the bathroom will make you forget that you’re on a ship, as it had double sinks, a soaking tub, a walk-in shower with amazing water pressure, and a toilet in a separate room.

There were also a couple of closet areas, so there was plenty of space to store luggage and clothes.

The suite then had a balcony that stretched the entire length of the suite, with very comfortable furniture.

Beyond the generally beautiful design, it has to be pointed out just how over the top everything was. I mean, the deck furniture uses fabrics from Loro Piana, just to give you a sense of just how high-end it is.

Housekeeping in the room was great (it was taken care of twice daily, and always well timed), butler service was very useful (more on that a bit later, when I talk about service), Starlink Wi-Fi was lightning fast, and I also love how Orient Express Sailing Yachts includes laundry. You could get unlimited washing, dry cleaning, etc., so that’s a very nice feature.

In the interest of checking out different suite products, I also had the chance to tour the Suite Panoramique, which is the entry level accommodation onboard, located on levels four and five. These are 506 square feet (47 square meters), so they’re spacious for an entry level suite on a cruise.

This had the same general design concept as the suite we were in, except there wasn’t a fully separate living area. The suite had a comfortable king size bed, a desk with a chair, a dining table, and a huge window with a double daybed of sorts.

While there was no bathtub, the bathroom still had double sinks, a walk-in shower, and a toilet in a separate room.

To point out the obvious, these entry level suites don’t have balconies. Of course people prefer to have balconies, but this is just a simple reality of the difference between sailboats and cruise ships, in terms of how many levels there are, how far above water they are, etc.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ top end suites are really next level, so I also had the chance to tour the Zephyr Suite, which is located on level seven, and is the second most premium suite onboard. This two bedroom suite has 2,486 square feet (231 square meters) of interior space, plus a terrace that’s 1,206 square feet (112 square meters).

What I thought was so cool was how unique the design of this suite was, as the top suite products seem to have a totally original design. This very much had a residential vibe, with a long hallway connecting the various parts of the suite.

However, perhaps the coolest feature was the replica of an Orient Express Heritage cabin, intended to pay homage to the legendary train.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has two pools onboard, with one being rather traditional, and one being unlike anything else at sea (at least to my knowledge). The main “leisure” pool is located on the fifth floor, at the back of the ship. While the pool has beautiful aesthetics and lovely deck space around it, this isn’t some destination pool in and of itself. So if a huge pool is a crucial factor in picking a ship, Four Seasons Yachts might be a better option.

We’re all different, and personally, I’m not much of a pool person. Quite to the contrary, I actually loved this pool deck, since it was mostly covered and in the shade, so I could nicely sit there and enjoy the breeze (funny enough, Four Seasons Yachts has an amazing pool, but I didn’t actually spend much time there, due to the lack of shade).

The ship then has a second pool, which is among the most memorable you’ll find on any ship. The lap pool is 54 feet (16 meters) long, and it’s located under the sails. It really feels like you’re in a cave, since it’s on a deck that’s one level down from the main upper deck. What a pool!

On the pool front, really my only disappointment was the lack of a hot tub. As much as I find hot tubs to be kind of gross, I do love them, especially on a ship, so I was sad there wasn’t one of those. In general, the newer ultra high end cruise lines seem to be lacking in that department (the same was true on Four Seasons Yachts).

Beyond the pool setup, on the seventh floor you’ll find a huge deck you can hang out on. There are lots of lounge chairs out here, though it’s not necessarily that popular for just lounging around. The star of the show here is what’s above.

The time when the deck really gets popular is when the ship pulls into or out of ports, given the panoramic views from up here, plus the ability to watch the sails be lowered and raised. I must say, it was absolutely mesmerizing to watch. They made a big event of departures, with live music, cocktails, etc. It really felt like a cocktail reception, only more intimate.

Speaking of deck space, another fun aspect of the ship is how you can actually just freely walk up to the deck in front of the bridge, and even all the way to the bow. How fun!

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian wellness complex is located on the fourth floor, and that includes a Guerlain Spa. This area is an impressive 5,380 square feet (500 square meters), with four treatment suites (including a double suite), as well as all kinds of other traditional spa facilities.

Guests can always use the facilities, even without an appointment, and that includes a sauna, steam room, relaxation area, locker rooms, etc.

The spa treatment rooms are absolutely gorgeous, whether we’re talking about the couples room, or the individual ones.

Ford and I got a couples massage during our final day (where we were at sea), and I can honestly say it was one of the best spa treatments I’ve ever had. Not only was the therapist I had incredible, but the massage bed was so comfortable, and there was something so calming about the view, the gentle sway of the ship, etc.

For those curious about the pricing, you can find part of the spa menu below.

The ship also has a full hair salon and barber shop, so there are no shortage of opportunities to get your grooming needs taken care of here. The barber shop even leads to the speakeasy — more on that later.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has a gym located on the fourth floor, which can be accessed by guests 24/7. The gym isn’t huge, but is more than sufficient given the size of the ship, in my opinion. Every time we used it, we were alone.

The gym had a good selection of cardio and weight equipment, as well as a separate room for aerobics, boxing, etc.

There was an excellent personal trainer onboard, and it was possible to schedule sessions with him at no extra cost. So it’s not just for group fitness, but even for personal sessions, on a space available basis. That’s really nice, as virtually any other cruise would charge for that, in my experience.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has an incredibly impressive entertainment area, located on deck four. The issue is, it’s not really used a whole lot. Now, I’m not sure I’d actually call this an “issue,” but let me explain.

When you think of mega cruise ships, nightly shows and entertainment are among the most popular attractions. The thing is, the smaller the ship is, the less interest there is in things like this, and that’s especially true for the cruise lines that are primarily targeted at people who haven’t historically been cruisers.

So the Corinthian has a huge theater with dozens of seats, but there’s not a whole lot that goes on there.

Perhaps the more interesting entertainment feature is the private cinema, where you can have them screen a movie (or whatever) for you.

There’s even a recording studio onboard — what a cool concept, and in addition to being able to play instruments here, I heard people have used this to record podcasts, etc.

On the topic of entertainment, the ship also has a card room on the fourth floor, with chess, checkers, decks of cards, etc.

Separately, there’s also the yacht club, which is basically a very elegant lounge area where guests can hang out, watch TV, etc.

Lastly, the ship has the library on the fourth floor, which has an incredible selection of books. Everything on the Corinthian is so thoughtful, including the book selection. As it was explained to us, the 1,500-book library is supposed to represent the most important books of the century, and were curated by the historic Parisian bookshop Galignani.

I know there’s sometimes confusion about whether Orient Express Sailing Yachts is kids friendly, and the answer is… sort of.

On most voyages, guests onboard must be 16 years of age or older. However, on dedicated family voyages, children ages six months to 15 years old are allowed as well. Infants under six months aren’t permitted onboard, and per the terms, “families traveling with little ones under two years old must be accompanied by a dedicated babysitter throughout their voyage.”

Quite honestly, it’s logical that Orient Express Sailing Yachts would have this policy, since the ship’s venues feel really intimate, the pools aren’t huge, etc.

For family voyages, the Corinthian does have a kids club onboard, which offers activities with a dedicated team. Babysitting services can also be arranged for excursions or gala evenings. But in terms of being kids friendly, I definitely think it’s an area where Four Seasons Yachts wins, as all voyages are kids friendly, the pool is huge, and there’s both a kids club and teens club.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has an incredibly impressive selection of restaurants, bars, and lounges onboard, with the culinary vision overseen by well-known chef Yannick Alléno. Before I get into details, let me just say that I found the quality of food and drinks onboard to be truly exceptional.

I try not to exaggerate, because I think far too many people are a little too generous when describing food on cruises (or flights, for that matter — what’s with all these people describing airplane food as Michelin dining?). However, I found the quality of catering on Orient Express Sailing Yachts to just be in a completely different league than Four Seasons Yachts.

I was also delighted by the generosity of the included options, with an incredible alcohol selection, caviar accompanying dishes at breakfast, lunch, and dinner (and even cocktails), etc. It’s also interesting to note that no reservations are allowed onboard, except at the fine dining restaurant that costs extra.

Everything was always available whenever we wanted it, though people will otherwise probably have mixed feelings on that policy (conversely, the issue when you do allow reservations is that people hog them and then just cancel at the last minute, leaving other guests with limited options).

Anyway, here are the most significant outlets onboard Orient Express Sailing Yachts:

With that out of the way, let’s get into the venues in a bit more detail.

La Terrasse is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ all-day dining restaurant, serving breakfast, lunch, and dinner. It’s located at the back of the sixth floor, and has both indoor and outdoor seating. The fact that this is the casual restaurant really tells you the quality of the experience, as there are white tablecloths all hours of the day.

This is the primary restaurant where breakfast is served, and you can find that menu below.

Breakfast is entirely a la carte, though at the start of the meal, a basket with a rotating selection of croissants and pastries was brought out.

There was a large selection of fresh juices and coffee available. My one disappointment was that the coffee was just okay, and clearly came from a machine. That’s ironic, because there’s plenty of delicious barista coffee on the ship, so this seems to be one of the only venues where that’s the case. Given the quality of service onboard, I’m sure they’d also be happy to get you a coffee from somewhere else, if you prefer.

We found the breakfast selection to be very good, and over the course of our stay tried the acai bowl with coconut and seasonal fruit, chia pudding with fresh mango, the mixed berry plate, the crispy and soft blinis with caviar cream and smoked salmon, the avocado toast, and more.

We also came to La Terrasse one day for lunch, and you can find that menu below.

We split the chickpea hummus with parmesan to start, and then had the smoked salmon club sandwich and Thai beef salad as our mains. At our server’s insistence, we finished off with a floating island for dessert. YUM.

We also had dinner here our first evening, and you can find that menu below.

To start, we had the smoked salmon with blinis and sour cream, and the gazpacho.

Then for mains, we had the pepper crusted beef fillet with cognac and cream sauce, and the red tuna teriyaki style, along with some sides.

Lastly, we finished off the meal with a selection from the cheese trolley, plus the vanilla millefeuille.

Across the board, the food and service were exceptional, so it’s amazing that this is just the most basic restaurant onboard, as it only gets better from there.

L’Ecrin is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ elevated dinner restaurant, with a focus on seafood and pasta. It’s located on the sixth floor, and it exclusively has indoor seating. This restaurant doesn’t cost extra, but in my opinion is on par with the paid restaurant on some of the other top ships.

We went here one evening for dinner, and you can find the menu below.

At the start of the meal, we were offered some sinfully delicious bread, along with some cured meats. I’ll talk more about service in a bit, but I might as well just mention in passing how good the crew was about our dietary preferences. For example, we mentioned when we boarded how we don’t eat pork, so without having to say anything, we were brought something that fit our needs.

We took an unusual approach to ordering. To start, we shared the seabass carpaccio with citrus marinade, and the spaghetti with caviar. My gosh, not only was the caviar portion on the spaghetti massive, but the overall flavor of the dish was incredible, as the beurre blanc combined with caviar had quite the unique flavor profile.

Then for mains, we had the warm lobster with olive oil and mayonnaise and the caponata and polenta. Again, this was very, very good.

For dessert, while I had heard amazing things about the suzette pasta (flambeed tableside), we decided on the signature bronte pistachio ice cream coupe, which was insanely indulgent.

What a meal! This was definitely my favorite restaurant onboard.

La Table by Yannick Alléno is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ most premium dinner restaurant, and it’s the only venue that comes at an extra charge, at the rate of €400 per person for the tasting menu.

First, we have to talk about the restaurant as such. Can you believe this is on a ship? This is without a doubt the most beautiful dining venue I’ve ever seen on a ship. With just over half a dozen tables, it’s also a really intimate space.

The tasting menu is constantly changing, and you can find the menu for our dinner below.

I’ll let the pictures speak for themselves…

The meal was very good, with service that matched the food quality. It really felt like a Michelin-starred dining experience in terms of the presentation, the service flow, etc.

While this was excellent, I will say, I wouldn’t necessarily feel compelled to dine here again. That’s just because the standard restaurants are so great that I don’t necessarily think it’s worth the incremental cost. At a minimum, don’t feel like you’re missing out if you don’t eat here… but definitely do take a look at the restaurant, to appreciate its beauty!

L’Encre is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ venue that’s exclusively open for lunch, and it was definitely my favorite lunch spot onboard. It’s basically a circular counter with a little over a dozen seats, so the setting is stunning.

You can find the menu below. Think of the concept as basically being like a seafood omakase, where they just keep bringing you out more dishes. Of course you can customize however you want, ask for more of whatever you really like, skip dishes, etc. Below is a sampling of what we ate.

La Piscine Lounge is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ poolside venue, serving drinks, snacks, and even full meals, throughout most of the day. It’s even opening at night, and can double as a bar for a pre-dinner drink. It’s a beautiful space, definitely not your typical pool bar!

You can find the drink list and menu for that below.

We had an afternoon snack here one day, and split the mezze and the veggie burger, both of which were very good.

Le Bar de la Bibliotheque is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ coffee shop in the library area, and it’s a lovely place from which to get some work done, read a book, etc.

Here you’ll find barista coffee, homemade cakes, fresh juices, kombucha, and more.

Le Wagon Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ primary bar venue, and it’s only open late at night. It’s intended to be a replica of the circular bar found on the modern Orient Express trains, with 1920s and 1930s heritage craftsmanship, so it’s a very cool space.

There’s a DJ there at night. The one thing to be aware of is that it only opens really late (9:30PM at the earliest, but often 10PM), and if you’re on a quieter sailing, there might not be too much of a vibe here. However, I’ve heard that on other sailings this place can be packed — it’s all about the crowd on a particular cruise.

I ordered the signature Corinthian Martini, with gin, vodka, champagne cordial, and — naturally, like everything on this ship — caviar!

Next, Le Speakeasy Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ speakeasy. The idea is basically that people do a bar crawl, and it’s common to move between both bars in the same evening. Much like Le Wagon Bar, this one also opens really late.

The bar is located through a hidden door in the barbershop, so they’re really committed to that speakeasy theme.

This bar even has a separate smoking room, which I’m sure smokers will appreciate (as it’s the only indoor space on the ship where you can smoke).

This bar also has some unique signature cocktails, and you can find that drink list below.

While not included, they are very proud of their liquor selection here, with some bottles that are older than my dad (and at a cost of up to $2,400 per shot — yowzers!).

Tempted as I was, I stuck to one of the included martinis. 😉

Le Flybridge Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ outdoor bar space located on the top floor. While this is open quite frequently, it really only gets busy when the ship sets sail, given the interest in watching the sails in action.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts of course has 24/7 room service, which is included, with no additional costs. The standard room service menu is on the basic side, but service very much falls into the category of them wanting to make guests happy, so they’re also happy to get you something from any restaurant, if you’d like (but since the menus are always changing, they’re not published in the room service menu).

We did have room service dinner one evening…

…and the final morning we had breakfast in our suite as well (we accidentally ordered too much).

Our amazing butler, Reuben, also gladly brought us cappuccinos and protein shakes, so they were happy to accommodate guests however they could.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has a very impressive included drink menu. You can find the standard alcoholic drink list below, though some venues have additional options or signature cocktails customized to that venue.

Having Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 as the house champagne is very impressive. And let me just say, they’re also not cheap with the pours — you can barely go anywhere without having a glass pushed on you. 😉

Of course there’s also a premium drink list with even more special wines and spirits, and those come at an extra cost.

I have to acknowledge that our sailing was rather empty, so the staff to guest ratio on this sailing was unreal. That being said, it wasn’t just the ratio that was amazing, but the quality of staff was really incredible as well. If you don’t have good staff, they’ll find a way to disappoint even if the staff to guest ratio is amazing.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that service on Orient Express Sailing Yachts was flawless in terms of attention to detail, and that was such a contrast to our Four Seasons Yachts experience.

It’s hard to even pinpoint any one area that impressed me, because it was just very consistent, polished, and proactive, across the board. Let me just give a few examples:

As I said in my Four Seasons Yachts review, while we had an amazing time, we had way more service issues than I’d consider to be acceptable, given the price point. This was exactly the opposite, and it was just flawless service experience after flawless service experience. So while I’m sure service is consistently good, I’m sure the empty sailing also contributed to taking this to the next level.

We were definitely on an odd sailing, in terms of seasonality, since we were on the second to last voyage before the ship sailed across the Atlantic, to start the winter season in the Caribbean.

Our sailing was empty, with just 19 of the 54 suites occupied, so there were fewer than 40 guests. It really felt like having a private yacht, as we rarely saw others, and we’d go to restaurants for dinner, at most a handful of other tables would be occupied.

On our sailing, almost everyone seemed to be a European retiree, so it was maybe in line with what you’d expect from the stereotypical guest profile of Orient Express trains. However, Ford has had some clients on Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and based on the feedback he has gotten, the ship can be an absolute scene, with some pretty over-the-top people.

The guest profile that Orient Express Sailing Yachts gets is probably a bit different than almost any other cruise line. For one, the ship has already been chartered multiple times in its first season, so you can imagine the kinds of people we’re talking about. And even on sailings that haven’t been chartered, there have been some A-list people onboard.

So anyway, we had a very pleasant, understated crowd onboard, but I’ve also heard the crowd can make for quite some people watching, especially for sailings in the South of France, etc.

As I said at the beginning, my goal here is to be as objective as possible, so what feedback do I have? Honestly, as much as I have a critical eye, I think there are shockingly few areas for improvements. Here are the things that stood out to me:

I also want to acknowledge that Trek Trendy had published a review of the Orient Express Corinthian, and I think that’s worth watching for a different perspective. I think he was being totally fair with some of his critique, but I had a different experience:

I travel a ton, and as much as I have so many amazing experiences, I’m almost always excited to go home, given that I miss family, and travel is sort of my “job.” I have to be honest, the Orient Express Corinthian was the first time in recent memory where I thought to myself “man, I wish it weren’t over.”

Earlier this year I experienced Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection and Four Seasons Yachts, and they’re both great in their own ways. However, Orient Express Sailing Yachts is really in a different league. Yes, it’s priced at the top end of the market, but it also includes the most, and I really appreciate that. There’s something nice about paying a high voyage cost in advance, but then feeling like everything is included.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts really is an unbelievable product, from the design of the ship, to the incredible restaurant and bar concepts, to the service. If you can swing it — and especially if you’ve never taken a cruise before — I can’t recommend this enough.

What’s your take on the Orient Express cruise concept?

Timely review as I coincidentally saw the Corinthian tendering in Marigot (Saint Martin) this morning. The crew had set up a buffet of cold drinks at the marina for the returning guests. The tender was loaded which fresh flowers, possibly for a wedding. Even from the distance, the Corinthian looks magnificent.

I just want to thank you for being honest and up front about this cruise be comped by the provider and I have every confidence it won't influence your review. I'm just surprised that on all of Ford's previous luxury cruises which you reviewed he was not offered a travel agent discounted rate and had to pay full fare. Travel Agents are indispensable to cruise lines, not so much as advisors, but as a distribution medium, even with commissions, less expensive than building up their own staff to support direct bookings. So, in that regard, as an incentive they offer travel agents generous discounts as well as "fam trips" such as this one.

Well this is the first time I've read a cruise review and wanted to do it. Perhaps one day...

So a 4 day cruise for 2 with terrace is 29k EUR in May 2027... aside from the price, looks amazing.

It’s funny that a lot of the highlights of the room etc are that “you forget you are on a ship”. What is the point of this over being in a nice hotel in a nice city. Especially if you only visit and disembark in one city?

#6026. House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

“My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

“We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

“I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”

It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

“Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack said in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he said at Thursday’s meeting.

#6024. How Many Miles Per Gallon Does A Boeing 747 Get?

Phillip B. Espinasse | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

With its four engines, the Boeing 747 uses vast quantities of fuel, burning through 3,800 gallons every hour. This high fuel burn amounts to 0.9 gallons used every second and 0.19 miles per gallon (mpg). In this article, we will detail the Boeing 747's mpg further, including the mpg per traveler, and how this compares to travel in a car and in modern airliners.

We will also delve into ongoing debates around sustainable aviation fuel to explore if aviation can be sustainable. After all, all airliners burn through staggering quantities of fuel.

According to the BBC's Future Planet, a cruising 747 burns through 0.9 gallons (four liters) of fuel each second. This is equivalent to 3,500 gallons (13,250 liters) of fuel every hour. If a 747 is cruising at its standard cruising speed of around 580 mph (933 km/h), it is covering a mile every 6.2 seconds.

Covering a mile requires 5.9 gallons of fuel. As a result, a cruising Boeing 747 can achieve just 0.18 miles per gallon. However, this is not the full picture, as a 747 carries far more people than most aircraft. For example, Qantas' 747-400s carried 364 passengers across three classes.

If we extrapolate this number of seats into the mpg that each passenger has, the data shows 65.5 mpg per passenger. According to calculatormpg.co.uk, the baseline for a good car mpg is 50. If a car is carrying two people, then the car is achieving 100 passenger miles per gallon.

This suggests that flying on a 747 still uses substantially more fuel than a car carrying multiple people, but less than a car carrying one person. The other difference to consider when comparing fuel consumption across modes of transport is that a 747 has to take off, which is not a concern for a car or train.

Takeoff is the most fuel-intensive part of any flight as the jet has to get up to speed while it is at its heaviest, and then climb to cruising altitude. The exact fuel consumption during takeoff depends hugely on how close the aircraft is to its maximum takeoff weight (almost a million pounds). However, the general quantity of fuel needed is approximately 5,000 gallons (19,000 liters).

This consumption of fuel equates to a fuel burn of approximately 154,000 lbs (70,000 kg) for a flight from London to New York. To sustain such a high consumption, a 747 can carry a vast amount of fuel. The debut 747 could carry 48,400 gallons (183,000 liters) of fuel. Later variants increased this capacity to 63,034 gallons (238,610 liters) for the 747-8.

This vast ocean of fuel is stored primarily in the aircraft's wings. A 747 has two main fuel tanks in each wing, with further reserve fuel tanks in the wings' outer sections and central wing tanks. It is common for airliners to store fuel in the wings to free up fuselage space for cargo storage.

The primary fuel tanks are usually filled first. Any further fuel needed for the flight is put into the central wing tank. Any final drops needed are pumped into the reserve tanks. Select 747 models can increase fuel capacity further by sealing off part of the horizontal stabilizer and using it as an additional auxiliary tank.

In recent years, the 747-400F's fuel storage has come under FAA scrutiny due to improperly applied cap seals on some aircraft. Should these seals fail during a lightning strike or short circuit, it could allow arcing within the fuel tanks and cause an explosion.

The FAA's attention came following several fuel tank explosions on commercial aircraft in the late 1990s. This led to a 2001 review titled ‘Transport Airplane Fuel Tank System Design Review, Flammability Reduction, and Maintenance and Inspection Requirements.’

The document led to a range of safety recommendations, including those relating to cap seals. In June 2022, the FAA responded to reports that cap seals were not being applied properly during production of the 747-400F. A design change omitted the application of the cap seals on eight fasteners, distributed equally across both wings.

At a surface level, the similar MPG per traveler between a 747 and a modern car would suggest a similar amount of environmental harm. Moreover, the US Energy Information Administration claims that jet fuel produces 21.1 lbs of CO2 per gallon, which is comparable to the 19.6 lbs of greenhouse gas produced from burning a gallon of gasoline.

However, focusing on CO2 alone hides the unique environmental harm caused by burning aviation fuel at altitude. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change points to the effects of water vapor clouds that contain black carbon, nitrous oxide, and sulfur dioxide.

Climate scientists use 'radiative forcing' as their measure for how environmentally harmful an activity is. A 2010 study by the University of Oslo’s International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis compared the radiative forcing of car and aircraft travel. The scientists concluded:

"Air travel results in a lower temperature change per passenger-kilometer than car travel on the long run; the integrated radiative forcing of air travel is on short- to medium time horizons much higher than for car travel. Per passenger-hour traveled however, aviation’s climate impact is a factor 6 to 47 higher than the impact from car travel."

One reason the 747 burns so much fuel and has a poor mpg, causing greater environmental harm, is that it's an outdated airframe. This aircraft was first introduced in 1970, and the technology available 56 years ago was substantially less advanced than aircraft technology today.

As a result, the 747 would be considered incredibly inefficient if it were produced today. Furthermore, modern airliners are far lighter than the 747, needing less fuel for takeoff. 21st-century widebody, and notably two-engine, aircraft are far more efficient due to modern technology.

They burn less fuel. However, because they carry fewer passengers than the behemoth 747, they don't necessarily have a better mpg per passenger. The Airbus A350 was introduced in 2015 with Qatar Airways, becoming the first Airbus aircraft constructed primarily with carbon-fibre-reinforced polymers.

Simple Flying reported that this aircraft burns 2,700 gallons per hour, or 0.75 gallons per second. With a cruising speed of 561 mph, the aircraft travels a mile every 6.4 seconds and has a cruising mpg of 0.208. Qantas's upcoming A350-1000s will have 238 seats across four classes, yielding an mpg per passenger of 50. This is equivalent to a modern car with only the driver on board.

A Boeing 787 Dreamliner has also advanced the field of environmentally conscious aviation. The Dreamliner was first introduced in October 2011 with All Nippon Airways. This jetliner burns 2,900 gallons of fuel per hour, and its cruising speed is 561 mph. As a result, the aircraft burns 5.17 gallons per mile, yielding an mpg of 0.193. Meanwhile, a Qantas 787-9 Dreamliner has 236 seats across three classes, so each passenger gets 44.8 mpg during the cruise.

We can see that even modern airliners consume vast quantities of fuel, causing significant environmental harm. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) could be a pathway to mitigate the harm of this enormous fuel consumption. SAF is defined as aviation fuel that is not derived from fossil fuels, but has near-identical performance characteristics.

It can be mixed with conventional fuel, and aircraft don't have to be re-engineered. Its development has come with a host of benefits and challenges. IATA's criteria for fuel to be considered sustainable are that it must reduce CO2 emissions across its lifecycle, not require excess freshwater, not compete with food production, and not cause deforestation.

If SAF can be rolled out, it could transform the aviation sector's sustainability. A ScienceDirect study based on the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation found that SAF could allow greenhouse gas emissions to decrease by up to 94%. Airbus puts this number closer to 80%.

SAF has begun to be seen in action within the commercial aviation sector. Virgin Atlantic operated the first 100% SAF flight in 2023, flying a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines. Rolls-Royce has since claimed to be the only engine manufacturer to confirm that all its powerplants work with SAF.

However, SAF rollout has not yet been substantial, primarily due to economic challenges: SAF costs an average of $6 per gallon, while fossil-fuel-based jet fuel typically costs $2.29 per gallon (although it has been on the rise amid the Iran War). The high cost is primarily due to low production rates, as just 33 million gallons of SAF were produced in the US in 2021. The US Department of Energy estimated in 2022 that SAF production would have to increase to 3 billion gallons annually.
