Avelo Airlines is offering a special early Black Friday deal for members of "Plus" — the carrier's paid loyalty membership program that costs $59 for the first year (and $99 per year after).

You can get 90% off base fares on select flights for travel through April 20, 2027.

No code is needed, but as stated, you'll need to be a Plus member.

The sale ends the night of Nov. 25, 2026.

BermudAir and its affiliate AnguillAir are offering 30% off flights to Bermuda and Anguilla for Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday when you use promo code "BLACK30" for travel dates between Dec. 1 and April 30, 2027. (Blackout dates apply.)

You can also get 75% off the base fare when you bundle flights and hotels with BermudAir Holidays when visiting Bermuda, Anguilla, Belize, Providenciales, South Caicos and Guatemala.

Breeze Airways has a Black Friday sale that gets travelers as much as $100 off round-trip flights when using the promo code "WISHLIST" from Friday, Nov. 27 through Sunday, Nov. 29. That's up to 60% off its base fares.

British Airways has flight and vacation deals for travel from the U.S. to London and several other top European destinations. Round-trip coach fares start at $623 and span across many dates. Customers can also save on vacation packages.

Delta will be offering a big Cyber Monday sale on Monday, Nov. 30, lasting through Dec. 2. Stay tuned for more details. Meanwhile, Delta already has some holiday offers available now.

Delta SkyMiles members can boost their rewards balances by earning bonus miles — at a rate of up to 5 miles per dollar spent — on Delta gift card purchases of $400 or more.

The United Arab Emirates' national carrier is offering discounts of up to 20% across many of its routes, bookable through Dec. 1.

Fiji Airways is offering Black Friday deals, with flights as low as $899 round-trip on nonstop flights from Dallas, Los Angeles and San Francisco to Nadi, Fiji, and then on to Sydney and Auckland.

JetBlue is offering one of its biggest sales of the year this Black Friday, including flights for as few as 3,200 JetBlue TrueBlue points.

BlueFirst — JetBlue's first-class awards — start at fewer than 20,000 points each way. You can also score as much as $800 off vacation packages.

Qatar Airways is offering up to 25% off fares through Nov 29, 2026, for travel from now through Oct. 31, 2027 (with some blackout dates).

There are a few additional promotions right now, too.

Singapore Airlines will host a fun Black Friday sale, with details to be released soon. The airline usually offers discounts of between 15% and 20% on all cabins from U.S. cities to Asia.

TAP Air Portugal is offering some great deals on fares to Europe from various U.S. airports. Prices start at $226 each way in economy, and there are some deals in business class. The sale ends Dec. 2.

Southwest has a Cyber Week sale, with details to be released after Black Friday. In the meantime, the airline told TPG: "From Nov. 20 through Dec. 3, customers can save on Getaways by Southwest® vacation packages, hotels, rental cars, and cruises, with Cyber Week offers that can help make the next getaway even more rewarding."

United Airlines is expected to offer Cyber Week deals. Stay tuned for more details in the days ahead.

Virgin Atlantic is likely to have some great deals for travel to the U.K. or Europe, but we don't have details yet. We'll update this post when we get those.

#5986. Airbnb Rates Rose After California Required Upfront Pricing—Research Shows Guests Still Benefit

California required Airbnb to put mandatory fees into the price travelers see up front. A new study of San Francisco and San Diego listings finds rates rose 4.8% relative to cities outside the mandate. The researchers still conclude guests came out ahead. Being able to figure out what you’re buying has value. A cheaper-looking listing isn’t necessarily a cheaper stay. The rental with the lowest headline price isn’t necessarily the one you’d choose if you could compare them properly. Back in 2022, when Airbnb introduced a toggle to show the price including fees, I wrote that guests shouldn’t have to turn it on. Showing what a stay costs ought to be the default. (And why would you toggle it off except for research purposes?) Ultimately hiding charges punishes honest businesses. The property showing its full price looks more expensive than the competitor holding something back until later. You make the customer click through every listing and do the math just to find out what a property costs, which makes it costly to compare. I’ve even covered a rental on Booking.com with a $1,000 destination fee, on top of a resort fee and cleaning fee – listed in the fine print. The Fees Became Easier To See. The Stays Didn’t Get Cheaper. The November working paper compares entire-home listings in the two California cities with matched properties in Seattle and Chicago, using July 2023–July 2025 data. Its price measure includes cleaning charges, but excludes Airbnb’s service fee and taxes. Listings more dependent on cleaning fees as a portion of total price were more likely to exit the platform. Higher quality listings were more likely to remain, while new listings offered lower fees and prices than incumbents. That creates an opportunity for hosts who were already offering a good deal. If you build cleaning into your rate while the place next door breaks it out, your property can look overpriced. Put both totals on the screen and you may be able to charge a higher rate while still offering a lower total price than competitors. There can also be fewer rentals competing for the same guests if enough hosts leave. That’s a reason not to assume that forcing everyone to advertise total price will lower prices. Limits To The Model Holding the available properties fixed, the paper’s model finds higher prices more than wipe out the direct gains from disclosure. Changes in the rental pool flip the result positive. Hotels aren’t included. Excluding storm-affected comparison months also reduces the estimated rate increase to 2.9%. Someone returning to the same property at a higher price might be worse off. Someone who avoids a bad value rental, or finds a better one once the prices are comparable, can benefit even while spending more. If an Airbnb becomes too expensive, the alternative isn’t necessarily another vacation rental. It might be a hotel, a different neighborhood, or deciding not to take the trip. The model also leaves out time saved searching. Anyone who’s clicked through 20 listings just to assemble a usable set of prices knows that’s worth something, too. The estimate of how much better off people are takes more assumptions than observing what happened to rates. A Cleaning Cost Can Be Real Without Being A Surprise Cleaning a house after a two night stay can cost about as much as cleaning it after a week. There’s a reason longer stays can be cheaper per night. Showing the full price doesn’t stop a host from accounting for that. Say one property charges $150 a night plus $150 for cleaning. Another charges $210 a night with cleaning included. For two nights, the first costs $450 and the second $420, before other charges. For a week, the first is cheaper. A search where you’ve already entered your dates can show the right comparison without making you calculate it yourself. Airbnb finally made total price display standard worldwide in April 2025, generally before taxes. The study looks back at California moving earlier to help understand the effect of the change. I’ve rented homes on Martha’s Vineyard and when visiting family outside Australia’s Gold Coast. A whole house can make more sense than hotel rooms for a family or group. Airbnb also now even says that the cleaning fee actually buys the cleaning, limiting the chores hosts can require. I once paid $300 a night for an Airbnb with a locked plastic box over the thermostat. You still have to be careful out there! #5985. A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?

The serious issues underneath an unserious moral panic

Demonstrators hold signs depicting George Floyd during a protest against police brutality and racial inequality in Brooklyn, N.Y., June 13, 2020.

Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a new project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”

Playbill has since released an apology claiming it “incorrectly approved” the job posting for its site, and is now reviewing its internal processes. “We know this listing has upset and offended many, and the fact that it made it onto our site has disappointed those who trust us as an outlet. For that, we are sorry, and are committed to regaining your trust,” the statement reads. In response to the post, some people have demanded that Playbill take more accountability by explaining exactly how such a thing was approved for the site, expose who is behind the musical (though that was already public), hire more minorities to prevent similar wrongdoing in the future, and issue apologies to the Floyd family and the black community. Others have more firmly called for barring the musical’s creative leader from the platform entirely.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

On “A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?”

#5984. American Airlines Passengers Restrain Man Who Went For The Door As Flight Attendant Blocks Him With A Drink Cart

Sean Bennett was asleep a few rows back on American Airlines’ San Diego–Chicago redeye when he heard a flight attendant yelling for a man to get away from the door. Passengers rushed up front to help. A second witness says a flight attendant pushed a drink cart up the aisle to keep the struggle from spilling back into the cabin. Bennett posted several videos from his seat. People crowded into the forward galley and got zip ties around the man’s wrists as he kept resisting almost until they landed. American Airlines flight 1494 took off from San Diego at 10:53 p.m. Pacific on Tuesday, November 24. About 40 minutes later, up at around 34,000 feet, it turned right for Phoenix. Police say the man had left his seat, walked to the front and repeatedly ignored instructions to sit back down. Passengers thought the man was trying to “take over the plane.” One report says he went for the cockpit door, but pilots told American’s operations center the man “tried to open the cabin door.” This was reported as a Level 3 threat which means life-threatening behavior. An attempt to breach the cockpit is Level 4. The man wound up on the ground in his underwear in the galley. At altitude, cabin pressure holds an exterior door shut. The Asiana Airlines passenger who actually opened an Airbus A321 exit was able to do it because the aircraft had descended enough on final approach. On another American flight to Chicago in 2024, Zach Etkind (‘the Wonton Don’) and five other passengers wrestled a man into the aisle after he went for an exit. They used duct tape and flex cuffs and the pilots went back to Albuquerque. This time the Airbus A321 landed in Phoenix around 1 a.m. Wednesday morning. Police met it at the gate. The man went to the hospital with a minor injury. The passenger who shared video of the inflight incident reports that he was upgraded on his next connection. Bennett posted several videos from his seat. People crowded into the forward galley and got zip ties around the man’s wrists as he kept resisting almost until they landed.

American Airlines flight 1494 took off from San Diego at 10:53 p.m. Pacific on Tuesday, November 24. About 40 minutes later, up at around 34,000 feet, it turned right for Phoenix. Police say the man had left his seat, walked to the front and repeatedly ignored instructions to sit back down.

Passengers thought the man was trying to “take over the plane.” One report says he went for the cockpit door, but pilots told American’s operations center the man “tried to open the cabin door.”

This was reported as a Level 3 threat which means life-threatening behavior. An attempt to breach the cockpit is Level 4. The man wound up on the ground in his underwear in the galley.

At altitude, cabin pressure holds an exterior door shut. The Asiana Airlines passenger who actually opened an Airbus A321 exit was able to do it because the aircraft had descended enough on final approach.

On another American flight to Chicago in 2024, Zach Etkind (‘the Wonton Don’) and five other passengers wrestled a man into the aisle after he went for an exit. They used duct tape and flex cuffs and the pilots went back to Albuquerque.

This time the Airbus A321 landed in Phoenix around 1 a.m. Wednesday morning. Police met it at the gate. The man went to the hospital with a minor injury.

#5981. What We Leave Out When We Talk About Sexism in Science

The research on bias against women in STEM is far more mixed than the headlines suggest.

Imagine you’re a young woman considering a career in science. You’ve heard that when a man and a woman with identical qualifications apply for the same job, hiring committees tend to favor the man. You ask for evidence, and someone sends you a study. It’s a real study, published in a prestigious journal, and it says more or less what you were told. Case closed?

Steve Stewart-Williams is a professor of psychology at the University of Nottingham Malaysia.

On “What We Leave Out When We Talk About Sexism in Science”

#5980. Bilt Palladium Is My Best Card For Everyday Spending—Get It By December 31 To Lock In Its Most Valuable Rewards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Bilt is changing how its credit cards earn rewards, and cardholders who want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash on everyday spending need to make a choice. I’ve already opted to keep the benefit—it’s a big reason my Bilt Palladium gets most of my spending.

If you don’t have a Bilt card, I’d get one now. You need to apply, get approved and accept the card offer by December 31, 2026 to preserve the choice of earning 4% Bilt Cash. Existing cardmembers also need to actively choose to keep it before their first card anniversary in 2027. Doing nothing means moving into the new rewards structure.

The Bilt Palladium Card gets the majority of my spending. I pay my mortgage through Bilt, but the card would be valuable to me even without a housing payment that can earn points.

I’ve written that Palladium looks complicated, but it’s the best everyday rewards card.

I consider these the most valuable points. You can redeem them at 1.25 cents apiece through Bilt’s travel portal, but I usually want to transfer them. The transfer partner lineup gives me access to:

Most transfers are 1:1. Accor is 3:2, I Prefer is 1:2, and Amtrak is 2:1. Bilt also runs large Rent Day transfer bonuses, often with better offers for higher elite tiers. I’ve used bonuses for transfers to Japan Airlines, British Airways, Virgin Atlantic and Air France KLM. Earning points quickly and then transferring with a bonus is why I want so much of my spending here.

Bilt is changing the earning choice in 2027. Today, cardmembers can choose:

Most cardmembers already choose the second option. Palladium is still a great card that way. But for most people putting significant spending on the card, especially when they’re generating more Bilt Cash than their housing payments would consume, I think the 4% option is much more valuable. Once you’ve reached the highest housing multiplier, spending more doesn’t increase that multiplier. With Flexible Bilt Cash, more spending keeps producing more Bilt Cash to use.

There are exceptions. I’ve explained how the housing option can produce an effective 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. At the 25% spending threshold, $1,000 of everyday spending and $4,000 of eligible housing payments earn 2,000 points from the purchases and 2,000 from housing. That’s 4,000 points against $1,000 of everyday spending. The relationship between your spending and housing payments determines which choice works best.

For me, the accelerators alone are a reason to preserve Bilt Cash earning. Spend $200 in Bilt Cash to activate one and you earn an extra point per dollar on the next $5,000 in eligible spending. Palladium’s 2X becomes 3X. That $5,000 also generates another $200 Bilt Cash, which can fund the next accelerator. Each eligible cardholder can activate five per calendar year.

My wife and I have both maxed out our accelerators this year: 3 points per dollar on $50,000 of combined spending. We’ve earned points on housing payments as well.

She has an authorized user card on my Palladium account. It costs $95 annually and comes with her own Priority Pass membership. She doesn’t receive a second set of my annual hotel and Bilt Cash credits, but she can earn rewards in her own Bilt account (or I can switch it to mine).

I’ve laid out how my wife and I use this. I directed the points and Bilt Cash from her spending into her account instead of mine. She earns her own status, funds her own accelerators, and can take advantage of transfer bonuses separately. When an offer bonuses transfers of up to 100,000 Bilt Points per member, two accounts give us room to bonus 200,000 points, with each person’s bonus determined by their own status.

An authorized user’s spending doesn’t automatically get the primary cardholder’s active accelerator. They need to activate their own, using their own Bilt Cash. Bilt also gives the primary cardholder separate card numbers and controls over authorized user spending, including transaction and monthly limits. You can add an authorized user starting at age 13. But for my wife and me, the separate rewards accounts are the reason this has been so useful.

And I’ve gotten far more out of Bilt Cash than just faster points earning. I’ve redeemed it for:

For my everyday spending, Palladium earns the points I want faster than any other card, and the benefits have been incredible. The new structure still allows Palladium and Obsidian cardmembers to use accelerators. Palladium’s $400 annual hotel credit and $200 annual Bilt Cash become a $600 annual Bilt Cash deposit at the card anniversary. That can fund three accelerators. Members can also earn Bilt Cash from other activity, including $50 for each 25,000 qualifying points. But they won’t replenish it at 4% of everyday spending.

Keeping the existing structure also preserves my separate $200 hotel credits, which I can stack with Bilt Cash hotel redemptions. The Bilt Cash hotel redemption allowance moves from monthly to twice yearly starting January 1 even for those keeping 4% earning, but I can still get the two $300 discounts this way.

Plus, Bilt Cash now expires at the end of the month 12 months after it’s earned. Cash earned in February 2026 lasts through February 28, 2027. The old rule would have wiped out everything over $100 at year-end. Having more time to use what I earn makes the 4% option better for me.

If you don’t have a card, I’d apply now and complete approval and acceptance before December 31. My choice is Bilt Palladium. The ability to preserve 4% Bilt Cash also applies to the Bilt Obsidian Card (See rates and fees) and no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (See rates and fees).

And if you already have a card, don’t assume your current selection of Flexible Bilt Cash protects you from the change. You need to proactively choose to keep it. I’ve already done this:

The new rewards model is selected by default.

You have until your first card anniversary in 2027 to make that election. Preserve it now and you can still move to the new structure later. Once that switch takes effect, you can’t move back. That’s why getting a Bilt Palladium Card now makes so much sense – keeping the earning option. They’ll pry the 4% Bilt Cash earning option from my cold, dead hands, as they say.

#5979. Your complete guide to the ALL Accor hotel loyalty program

Answer a few questions and get your top card matches for earning maximum rewards.

ALL Accor reward points have a fixed value when you redeem them toward eligible hotel stays: 1,000 points get you 20 euros off. That gives each reward point a hotel stay value of 2 euro cents and is why TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Accor points at 2.25 cents.

ALL Accor reward points expire after 365 consecutive days without eligible point-earning activity. Any qualifying activity that credits at least one reward point extends the validity of your entire balance for another 365 days. An eligible donation of reward points can also extend the validity of your balance.

ALL Accor doesn't price hotel awards as traditional free nights. Instead, you can generally redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay. When redeeming online, you can use 1,000 points for 20 euros off or 2,000 points for 40 euros off; after that, redemption amounts generally increase in increments of 2,000 points.

You can earn ALL Accor Silver, Gold or Platinum status through either status nights or status points within a calendar year. Silver requires 10 nights or 2,000 status points, Gold requires 30 nights or 7,000 status points, and Platinum requires 60 nights or 14,000 status points. Diamond status requires 26,000 status points and can't be earned through nights alone, while Limitless status is available by invitation only.

An eligible stay paid for in part or in full with reward points can still earn status nights. However, you'll only earn reward points and status points on the eligible portion of the bill that you pay without reward points.

Accor may not have the same name recognition or footprint in the U.S. as some other major hotel groups, but its portfolio may be difficult to ignore if you travel internationally. Its brands range from luxury names such as Raffles and Fairmont to budget-friendly options such as Ibis.

The ALL Accor loyalty program works differently from many hotel programs familiar to U.S. travelers. Reward points have a fixed value in euros toward most eligible hotel stays, elite status can be earned through nights or eligible spending, and paid memberships can help you save on stays and accelerate your progress toward status.

Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming ALL Accor points, qualifying for elite status and deciding whether the program is a good fit for you.

ALL Accor is the hotel loyalty program for Accor Group. The program covers over 5,800 hotels across more than 45 brands in 110-plus countries worldwide, ranging from Fairmont and Pullman to Mercure and Ibis.

Accor has an especially strong footprint in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region. Its comparatively limited North American footprint makes ALL Accor less appealing to many U.S.-based travelers.

You can become a member of ALL Accor by visiting the program's website and clicking the sign-up button in the upper-right corner. From there, it's a quick and easy process to sign up for the free-to-join ALL Accor program.

You'll see two different points balances in your ALL Accor account: reward points and status points. Reward points are what you can redeem for stays and other rewards, while status points are one of the ways you can earn ALL Accor status.

When you book an eligible stay — which generally excludes stays booked through online travel agencies — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, as well as status points based on the brand and your eligible pretax spending.

Specifically, here's how many reward points and status points you'll earn per 10 euros (about $11) spent:

So, a Classic member staying at an Adagio Access property would earn 500 reward points and 500 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending, while a Diamond elite member would earn double the reward points but the same number of status points. Meanwhile, 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending at a Fairmont would earn 2,500 status points regardless of elite tier, but a Classic member would earn 2,500 reward points while a Diamond elite member would earn 5,000 reward points.

Accor has more than 45 brands; here's an overview of the Accor Group brands:

However, not all of these brands participate fully in ALL Accor. The list of excluded hotels and brands is rather long, but note that no HotelF1 properties participate, most Ibis Budget properties are excluded and only select The Hoxton hotels participate.

ALL Accor also includes select third-party “Partner of ALL Accor” properties. Earning and elite benefits may vary at these hotels, and reward points can't be used to reduce the cost of stays at IntercityHotel, Steigenberger, Steigenberger Icon, Maxx, Jaz in the City or Zleep properties.

The ALL Accor hotel loyalty program has an entry tier, four earnable elite status tiers and an invitation-only Limitless tier. Members can also benefit from select paid memberships and occasional status match or challenge opportunities.

Status nights and status points reset at the start of each calendar year. Once you reach a new tier, you'll keep it for the rest of that calendar year and the following calendar year. To retain it beyond then, you must requalify during the next calendar year.

ALL Accor members have Classic status if they don't qualify for elite status. So, as soon as you join ALL Accor, you'll enjoy Classic benefits, including:

You can earn ALL Accor Silver status when you stay 10 nights or earn 2,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Classic members, Silver elite members get the following perks:

If you happen to have Gold status with Qatar Airways Privilege Club, you can link your account with ALL Accor and upgrade to Silver status after your first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Gold status when you stay 30 nights or earn 7,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Silver elite members, Gold elite members get the following perks:

Some cards issued outside the U.S. offer ALL Accor Gold status as a cardmember perk, though none issued in the U.S. currently do. And Qatar Airways Privilege Club Platinum members can upgrade to ALL Accor Gold status after their first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Platinum status when you stay 60 nights or earn 14,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Gold elite members, Platinum elite members get the following perks:

Once you reach 60 nights or 14,000 status points within a calendar year, you'll earn two suite night upgrades. Each suite night upgrade guarantees a one-night upgrade to a suite. You can earn an additional suite night upgrade for every additional 4,000 status points you earn.

You can earn ALL Accor Diamond status when you accrue at least 26,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Platinum elite members, Diamond elite members get the following perks:

ALL Accor also has an invitation-only Limitless status, which Accor grants at its discretion. In addition to all the Diamond benefits, Limitless members get 24-hour access to a personal assistant and concierge service, can gift Platinum status to a person of their choice and can transfer reward points to as many as five other ALL Accor members (up to 12 transfers per year).

ALL Accor offers three paid ALL Accor+ memberships: ALL Accor+ Explorer, ALL Accor+ Voyager and ALL Accor+ Ibis.

These subscriptions offer discounts, a boost toward higher elite status and various other perks. Although ALL Accor+ subscriptions can be combined, ALL Accor caps the bonus status nights you can receive from subscription programs and cobranded cards at 30 per account, per calendar year.

I've considered buying the ALL Accor+ Ibis membership, as its 15% discount could cover the 99-euro annual fee once you spend about 660 euros on eligible stays booked at the subscription rate.

You have many opportunities to earn reward points and status points with Accor. Here's an overview of the options most relevant for U.S. residents.

When you book an eligible stay — which excludes stays booked through online travel websites — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, plus status points based on the brand and the cost of your stay. Specifically, Classic members earn reward points and status points as follows:

Elite members earn additional reward points on top of what Classic members earn; Silver members get 24% additional reward points, Gold members get 48% additional reward points, Platinum members get 76% additional reward points, and Diamond and Limitless members get 100% additional reward points. However, elite members don't earn any additional status points over what Classic members earn.

So, while a Classic member would earn 1,250 reward points and 1,250 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending on an Ibis stay, a Platinum member would earn 2,200 reward points and 1,250 status points on the same stay.

You'll earn reward points and status points not just for your room but also for meals, minibar, spa and other eligible charges to your room. Plus, if you opt to Skip the Clean, you'll earn 100 reward points per day skipped. And keep in mind that you can earn reward points — but not status points or nights — on day rooms at participating Accor properties.

You can earn reward points on rental cars from three partners as follows:

You can earn reward points by clicking through the Collections site before shopping.

You can earn up to 600 reward points on your first survey with Club Opinions. And with e-Rewards, you can earn 250 reward points on your first survey.

You can convert the following transferable rewards into ALL Accor reward points as follows:

Transfers are final, though, so make sure converting your rewards to ALL Accor is the best-value option before you transfer.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

You can earn reward points as follows when you convert select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards:

After linking your ALL Accor account with an eligible airline loyalty account, you may be able to earn reward points on select flights in addition to the rewards you earn with the airline program. For example, you can earn 1 reward point per $2 spent on eligible Qatar Airways flights and 1 reward point per 2 euros spent on eligible Air France-KLM flights.

Elite members with Gold status or higher in ALL Accor or Qantas Frequent Flyer can earn 1 reward point per 4 Australian dollars (about $3) spent on eligible Qantas flights, while ALL Accor members with Silver status or higher and Azul Fidelidade members with Diamante status can earn 1 reward point for every 7.50 euros spent on eligible Azul flights.

You can earn 1 reward point and 1 status point per 2 euros spent when you host a group of at least eight attendees (or at least eight rooms) at a participating hotel. It doesn't matter whether your event is a professional gathering or personal celebration.

You have plenty of options for redeeming Accor points. As with earning, we'll focus on redemptions most relevant to U.S. residents.

ALL Accor lets you redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay at a participating hotel. You can use points toward part or, in some cases, all of your stay, although some prepaid rates require a portion to be paid by card.

To redeem points for a hotel stay online, log in to your ALL Accor account and search for a stay as normal. When you choose a rate at a specific hotel, look for one with a purple "Pay with your points" designation if you want to redeem points for part or all of your stay.

Near the end of the booking process, you can opt to redeem points toward your stay. For example, I could redeem 1,000 points for 20 euros off my stay and pay the remaining balance with a credit card.

These hotel stay redemptions provide a fixed value of 2 euro cents per point, so you generally won't get outsize value from your reward points.

You can redeem — and, in some cases, bid — Accor points for select entertainment, dining and sports experiences through the ALL Limitless Experiences page. There are some great deals to be found, too, such as this Christmas Eve dinner for just 600 points.

You can also redeem Accor points for select activities through ALL Accor Activities & Events.

It's worth checking both of these programs periodically to see whether any experiences fit your upcoming schedule and tastes.

You can redeem your Accor reward points for select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards as follows:

I don't usually recommend transferring hotel points to other travel loyalty programs, as you'll typically lose a good bit of value. Check TPG's valuations and calculate your redemption rate before transferring ALL Accor points to another program.

ALL Accor is most compelling for travelers who frequently visit Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region, where Accor has a much larger footprint than in North America. Its hotel redemptions are also easy to understand: 1,000 reward points generally get you 20 euros off an eligible stay.

However, that simplicity means you generally won't find the outsize hotel redemptions that are possible with programs that use award charts or dynamic pricing. ALL Accor also lacks a U.S.-issued cobranded credit card, and its U.S.-accessible transfer partners generally transfer at less than a 1:1 ratio.

Elite status can still be useful, especially at the Platinum and Diamond levels, which offer perks such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast in certain regions or on certain days. Finally, ALL Accor+ subscriptions may be useful for some travelers.

ALL Accor probably won't be the best primary hotel program for most U.S.-based travelers given its relatively limited North American footprint, lack of a U.S.-issued cobranded card and less-than-1:1 transfer ratios. But it may be useful if you frequently stay at Accor brands in Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region.

Reward points are easy to use at a fixed value toward eligible hotel stays, while higher elite tiers offer potentially valuable benefits such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast. Frequent Accor guests should consider whether an ALL Accor+ subscription could pay for itself through discounts, status nights and other benefits.

Even if you don't plan to pursue status, it's worth joining ALL Accor before your next eligible stay to access member rates and earn reward points.

#5978. Trump, while wielding veto threat, sees possible deals with incoming Dem majority

President Donald Trump, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gestures during a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump said Friday he might get more accomplished with Democrats running the House and Senate than he did in a Republican-led Congress, but his legislative to-do list differs significantly from the incoming majority party.

After previously suggesting he could strike a bipartisan immigration deal with Democrats, Trump on Friday added several items to his wish list after returning Thursday night from a swing across Asia, including several that have support with Democrats with whom he’s bitterly clashed before.

Speaking in a stuffy James A. Brady Briefing Room for just shy of 90 minutes, the GOP president contended, without naming a single Democratic leader or lawmaker, that members of the opposition party have called him “about two things in particular,” pointing to health care and immigration.

“What's happened is I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he said of the 17 days since Democrats gained dozens of seats across the two chambers. “But people that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me.”

But Trump also reminded Democrats that he is more than willing to veto legislation he doesn’t agree with, calling it one of the “extreme powers” of his office and one he might use to bring them to the bargaining table.

“So they’re going to send things my way, and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things, and I’m going to veto them,” he said. “I think, after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ’I’m going to veto, unless you want to do this and this and this.”

He predicted House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely new speaker of the House, and Sen. Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., expected to become majority leader, would seek deals because both are “smart.” He would not say if he’d spoken to either leader, but called Jeffries “streetwise,” while noting he had once made a donation to Schumer earlier in their careers.

Trump went as far as to suggest working across the aisle on health care “may be easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation,” a reference to a fast-track process that allows sprawling bills to pass each chamber with a simple majority — legislation typically needs 60 votes to advance in the Senate.

The sports-loving president added the Senate-approved “Protect College Sports Act” to his list, and repeated his support for legislation to make Hollywood production companies more competitive. The House moved closer Friday to acting on an amended “Protect” bill when the Rules Committee posted a notice calling for any desired floor amendments by noon on Wednesday.

“We have to pass that bill,” Trump said. “Every college is going to go bankrupt if we don't get a bill because they're going crazy.”

The Senate’s “Protect” bill would establish the first federal regulatory framework for college athletics, setting national rules for name, image and likeness deals and compensation, as well as installing limitations on agents. It would put in place standards for NIL agreements, create guidelines for schools making direct payments to athletes and provide targeted antitrust protections to certain governing organizations.

He said the Senate bill has “tremendous bipartisan support,” but its path in the House remains unclear, according to lobbyists who have worked on the issue. That’s because some House conservatives oppose it and the Congressional Black Caucus has said its members would vote “no.”

The CBC has linked it to GOP efforts to redistrict majority minority districts in states the group, with its nearly 60 House members, contends would benefit most from the bill. The CBC is expected to be even larger in the next Congress, further complicating the “Protect” bill’s path to Trump’s desk.

Trump also pointed to the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act as another possible bipartisan bill. The legislation would establish a federal tax credit to encourage film and television productions to shoot in the United States rather than overseas. Some countries offer American film companies lucrative production incentives to shoot on their soil.

In a twist, Trump noted Sen. Adam B. Schiff — a longtime foe from the California Democrat’s days probing the president’s alleged ties to Russia as House Intelligence Committee chair during Trump 1.0 — supports that measure.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support. I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’”

But the president’s vision of a 120th Congress bipartisan agenda differs from what Democrats have promised.

Many Democratic incumbents and candidates promised voters they would pursue legislation to lower consumer prices, pare health care costs and end Trump’s Iran conflict, which the president again on Friday acknowledged hurt his party by increasing prices.

Jeffries, during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, pointed to reversing the administration’s Medicaid cuts, reviving the Affordable Care Act credits, ending the war and lowering costs as his conference’s “North Star” priorities. This week he also said he would seek to move an immigration-related bill “immediately,” and that the House would “hold the crooks accountable,” a nod to aggressive oversight both chambers are likely to engage in.

On Iran, reporters pressed Vice President JD Vance over his post-midterms X post blaming the war for the GOP wipeout. One reporter pressed Vance, a potential 2028 Republican presidential hopeful, whether he — like Trump — would start the conflict again. Vance sidestepped as he approached the lectern from behind Trump’s right shoulder, but did not give a full-throated endorsement to go to war again.

“The president has said he would do it again,” Vance replied. “And my view is that my goal is, and my job is to support the president of the United States.”

In a potential 2028 GOP primary preview, Secretary of State Marco Rubio — who has gained ground in some polls since the midterms — was expressionless as he stood a few feet away, positioned behind Trump’s left shoulder.

Trump’s midday press conference marked his first since voters handed Democrats at least 258 House seats and 56 in the Senate come Jan. 3. He again contended the outcome would have been different “if I were on the ballot,” and floated vague conspiracy theories about some falling prices since Democratic candidates bulldozed across the country.

At one point, he decided to make an announcement that he claimed he had not warned his staff about by floating a threat to U.S. companies that want to build data centers overseas.

​"We're going to put a tremendous tax on them, if they do it," he said, continuing his advocacy of erecting the unpopular facilities across the United States and willingness to use executive powers.

As he returned to Washington Thursday night, the White House touted on social media what it called $17 billion in new deals secured with Asian countries this week. Trump on Friday claimed he told Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his country would begin buying “100 percent” of its oil from the United States — and Marcos had said, “Yes, sir.”

White House aides handed out a one-page “declaration toward peace” before Trump arrived that he later said he had reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The three leaders agreed to ramp up production of petroleum products, pursue unspecified changes to the United Nations and a statement that a “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” according to the White House’s description of the declaration.

It also included a line about agreement on the “principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials,” an apparent show of support to Putin being targeted by international criminal entities over his conduct of his war with Ukraine. The U.S. president on Friday said such entities have “fake power.”

Trump called the declaration “formal,” as he lauded Chinese cities he was driven through this week as extremely “clean.” He compared them to some Democratic-run U.S. cities and states he described as “so embarrassing” and “dirty.” He dubbed Xi, considered by many Republican and Democratic lawmakers to be a dictator, a “great man.”

Some Republican lawmakers who will return for the 120th Congress said they have some reservations about Trump meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, doubting Putin’s and Xi’s sincerity about changing course on a number of issues.

Retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., went further Thursday.

“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and to China. And we stood up for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values,” Bacon, who has floated a potential 2028 presidential bid, said during a National Press Club event. “President Trump has been terrible on this right here."

“He has played footsie with Putin, he’s even blaming Zelenskyy for why the war started,” he added, referring to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “It infuriates me. And Ronald Reagan is rolling in his grave. … And now the Democrats are talking about the bad Russians and the bad Chinese, and we got to be tougher — it’s another role reversal, here.”

#5977. American Airlines May Hire A CEO Successor To Robert Isom Before End Of Year — Its Best Outside Candidate Is At Southwest

When Robert Isom became CEO of American Airlines in 2022, he never named another executive to replace him as president. Now former Wall Street Journal airline reporter Scott McCartney says conversations he’s had lead him to think “American is trying to bring in an outsider as president and heir apparent to CEO Robert Isom.” And he thinks a president could be named by year-end. That’s much more plausible than long-reported speculation that Isom would get replaced as CEO by the board. On Airlines Confidential, McCartney thinks Isom wants to turn American around and then hand it off. McCartney’s first suggestion is a good one: drive across town and talk to Southwest’s COO Andrew Watterson who’s reportedly been sidelined from the CEO path there. American existing chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, has already appeared to play much of the President role (albeit without full reporting lines tiering up to him). A New President Lets American ‘Try Before They Buy’ This is the board that watched Delta take American’s South American partner LATAM away from it in 2019. Doug Parker kept his job for another two and a half years. When he handed it to Isom, he stayed on as chairman. A board with that history can get comfortable with succession planning a lot more easily than with removing a CEO for poor performance. And – for all of the lingering complaints about Robert Isom – they’ve finally been turning around the airline’s value proposition. Vice Chair Steve Johnson, who ran commercial for 18 months after Vasu Raja left and oversaw the new Citi deal, retires at year-end. Chief Operating Officer David Seymour never got Isom’s old President job and is retiring with severance. Hiring a president lets the board try before it buys. Someone who has run a much smaller airline can be a credible candidate for this job even if you wouldn’t hand them American right away. But what portfolio would the president have? Isom just told employees that Seymour’s successor, JonCarlo Gulbranson, will report directly to him. He could change his mind. Nat Pieper Has Already Been Doing Much Of The Job McCartney says he’s hearing that American wants someone with Delta experience and nobody inside is ready yet. The first requirement would hardly rule out Pieper. Pieper ran Delta’s commercial business in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and India. He helped bring Alaska into oneworld and went on to run the alliance. He’s only been at American about a year, so still qualifies as an outsider. He’s the one explaining to employees why American has to fight United in Chicago. On the October earnings call, Pieper took analysts’ questions and walked investors through an 18.5% year-over-year increase in premium unit revenue. After the August reorganization, Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden reports to him alone, rather than jointly to him and the operating head. He’s led the process to purchase new widebody jets that’s expected to come to completion soon. None of that is unusual for a commercial chief, but in front of employees and investors he’s already doing much of a president’s job. You can see why Pieper’s name was already coming up around headquarters in February. He’s the only plausible internal successor today. The next step would be greater operational responsibility, and a greater role in finance. Who Would Be Worth Hiring From The Outside? Southwest COO Andrew Watterson wouldn’t even need to relocated, and he’s served as that airline’s chief commercial officer as well. He had responsibility for revenue for two years while running the operation. He’s had to both sell the schedule and run the flights. And he’s well-liked by employees. Paul Jacobson is McCartney’s other suggestion. If he gets passed over for Mary Barra’s job as CEO of General Motors, he could be available. Jacobson spent 23 years at Delta, from financial analyst to CFO. His team raised nearly $30 billion during the pandemic. American has plenty of debt, but its bigger problem is getting customers to pay a premium to fly it. While Delta did this, Jacobson wasn’t in charge of commercial or operations. And he already makes as much as Isom does. Contra McCartney, I’d put Peter Ingram ahead of Jude Bricker. McCartney mentions both, and both spent time at American. Ingram was Hawaiian’s CFO, commercial head and then CEO. He couldn’t turn Hawaiian around and sold it to American, but he wouldn’t be asked to become CEO on day one. And he ran a premium global airline, albeit a smaller one. Bricker was president of Allegiant Air, then ran Sun Country. He also took first class out of Sun Country’s planes. That may have been the right call for Sun Country but his record is running cost-focused operations, while American’s challenges are primarily around revenue rather than cost. Besides, Bricker just bought into Omni Air and became its CEO this month. He’d have to walk away from his own deal. The Delta executive I’d want is Glen Hauenstein. He spent nearly a decade as Delta’s president building precisely the premium revenue advantage American wants. He never got the CEO chair there. But he retired as president in February and agreed to advise Delta through year-end. But it’s not clear he’d come out of retirement for another president’s job without a date for the handover, and he’s older than Jacobson. I wasn’t a fan of Hauenstein, but he certainly understands the commercial side of the Delta business. However Hauenstein is not going to happen. His Delta non-compete appears to run through the end of 2028. Hauenstein retired as president on February 28, 2026. The agreement runs two years, but he’s continuing to receive payments as an advisor through the end of 2026. And Delta’s compensation plan specifically says that continuing to provide services as an independent contractor keeps the clock from starting unless the compensation committee decides otherwise. American Airlines is explicitly named in the non-compete, Hauenstein would lose his outstanding incentive awards, and the agreement lets Delta seek an injunction to stop him from taking the job. At Delta’s current share price, Hauenstein has an estimated $20 million in unvested incentives contingent on honoring non-compete (if Delta hits its targets). After the next round of payouts, that falls to $7.5 million. American could offer to make him whole, but they still risk a court enforcing the non-compete via an injunction to stop the hire. McCartney wonders whether the CEO search at GM was even triggered by American’s interest in Jacobson – deciding whether they want to give him the big chair or let him go. And McCartney gives long odds to another Delta alumnus, former operating head Jim Whitehurst, who is now a senior partner at Silver Lake and a United board member. There’s a cost to hiring any of them over Pieper. In 2016 American chose then-COO Isom for president and American’s President Scott Kirby went to United. Parker later told employees the board didn’t think it could keep both men, and they had to choose. Ten years later, the executive American is counting on to beat Kirby in Chicago is Nat Pieper. In deciding whether to hire him a new boss, the board has another moment of choosing. American has plenty of debt, but its bigger problem is getting customers to pay a premium to fly it. While Delta did this, Jacobson wasn’t in charge of commercial or operations. And he already makes as much as Isom does. Contra McCartney, I’d put Peter Ingram ahead of Jude Bricker. McCartney mentions both, and both spent time at American. Ingram was Hawaiian’s CFO, commercial head and then CEO. He couldn’t turn Hawaiian around and sold it to American, but he wouldn’t be asked to become CEO on day one. And he ran a premium global airline, albeit a smaller one. Bricker was president of Allegiant Air, then ran Sun Country. He also took first class out of Sun Country’s planes. That may have been the right call for Sun Country but his record is running cost-focused operations, while American’s challenges are primarily around revenue rather than cost. Besides, Bricker just bought into Omni Air and became its CEO this month. He’d have to walk away from his own deal. The Delta executive I’d want is Glen Hauenstein. He spent nearly a decade as Delta’s president building precisely the premium revenue advantage American wants. He never got the CEO chair there. But he retired as president in February and agreed to advise Delta through year-end. But it’s not clear he’d come out of retirement for another president’s job without a date for the handover, and he’s older than Jacobson. I wasn’t a fan of Hauenstein, but he certainly understands the commercial side of the Delta business. However Hauenstein is not going to happen. His Delta non-compete appears to run through the end of 2028. Hauenstein retired as president on February 28, 2026. The agreement runs two years, but he’s continuing to receive payments as an advisor through the end of 2026. And Delta’s compensation plan specifically says that continuing to provide services as an independent contractor keeps the clock from starting unless the compensation committee decides otherwise. American Airlines is explicitly named in the non-compete, Hauenstein would lose his outstanding incentive awards, and the agreement lets Delta seek an injunction to stop him from taking the job. At Delta’s current share price, Hauenstein has an estimated $20 million in unvested incentives contingent on honoring non-compete (if Delta hits its targets). After the next round of payouts, that falls to $7.5 million. American could offer to make him whole, but they still risk a court enforcing the non-compete via an injunction to stop the hire. McCartney wonders whether the CEO search at GM was even triggered by American’s interest in Jacobson – deciding whether they want to give him the big chair or let him go. And McCartney gives long odds to another Delta alumnus, former operating head Jim Whitehurst, who is now a senior partner at Silver Lake and a United board member. There’s a cost to hiring any of them over Pieper. In 2016 American chose then-COO Isom for president and American’s President Scott Kirby went to United. Parker later told employees the board didn’t think it could keep both men, and they had to choose. Ten years later, the executive American is counting on to beat Kirby in Chicago is Nat Pieper. In deciding whether to hire him a new boss, the board has another moment of choosing. McCartney says he’s hearing that American wants someone with Delta experience and nobody inside is ready yet. The first requirement would hardly rule out Pieper. Pieper ran Delta’s commercial business in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and India. He helped bring Alaska into oneworld and went on to run the alliance. He’s only been at American about a year, so still qualifies as an outsider.

He’s the one explaining to employees why American has to fight United in Chicago. On the October earnings call, Pieper took analysts’ questions and walked investors through an 18.5% year-over-year increase in premium unit revenue. After the August reorganization, Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden reports to him alone, rather than jointly to him and the operating head. He’s led the process to purchase new widebody jets that’s expected to come to completion soon.

None of that is unusual for a commercial chief, but in front of employees and investors he’s already doing much of a president’s job. You can see why Pieper’s name was already coming up around headquarters in February. He’s the only plausible internal successor today. The next step would be greater operational responsibility, and a greater role in finance.

I want flights that run on time without mechanical delays. Currently that seems to be impossible

It comes down to how best to deal with 2 existential crisis at AA:

1. Their dreadful finances 2. A workforce that understandably hates their lives

To consistently charge a premium that actually generates a profit, AA must solve both problems.

We can rely on the AA board to screw this up too! Parker’s hand-picked lap dogs haven’t made a decision since the merger in 2013. They are there for the benefits. Any real board would have ousted a CEO after the third DUI but Parker treated them to lifetime first class so he could have golf and drinking buddies. And deer in the headlights Isom has never had an original thought and is so insecure that he visibly shakes whenever Kirby speaks and he thinks innovation means copying 10 year old ideas. Small wonder AA sucks.

I feel like AA hired Isom’s successor a year ago – Nate Pieper. He’s been acting like the defacto CEO since that time. I feel like the last year has been the ‘try/buy’ period…the President title ought to come in the new year to make the succession plan obvious and public. It seems most public articulation of strategy in the last year has not come from Isom but rather from Pieper. Isom has seemed more of a pending emeritus exec than an actual leader. I suspect we’ll hear something by the start of Q2. I personally don’t see how bringing in a Hawaiian, Allegiant or Southwest exec have any experience nor relevance to what AA must do moving forward.

It sounds like you and Scott McCartney believe that employees don’t have a duty to do their jobs – that 100% of the blame for American’s obvious under performance rests with management. Don’t misunderstand, American’s management is responsible for its role in the dysfunction of the airline. But it’s only partially responsible. Labor is also responsible for its role.

The 2016 parallel runs deeper than Chicago. The executive the board let walk came back this spring with a merger pitch, which Kirby then shelved as off the table “for the foreseeable future.” APA, which triggered early contract negotiations in August, said at a Jefferies conference in June that it remained open to evaluating United’s approach and that American’s quick dismissal raised due-diligence concerns. So the heir’s real job is making the standalone case more compelling than Kirby’s if he comes calling again, with the pilots watching.

And at AA, morale is downstream of margin. The profit-sharing program now uses the same headline formula as Delta’s: 10% of the first $2.5B in adjusted pretax earnings, 20% above that. For 2025, Delta paid 8.9% of eligible pay; American paid 0.3%. Same formula, different airline.

P.S. Ingram sold Hawaiian to Alaska, not American, though American would be a homecoming for him: he spent 11 years at AMR, ending as American Eagle’s CFO. Fun wrinkle: two of your leading outside candidates have already been colleagues and competitors. Watterson ran planning and revenue management inside Ingram’s commercial organization at Hawaiian, then fronted Southwest’s 2019 Hawaii invasion as its revenue chief, with Ingram running Hawaiian. This industry doesn’t have a talent pool so much as a gene pool.

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 100,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

I added the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card to my wallet over 10 years ago for its simple earning rates and modest $95 annual fee.

It has remained a valuable mid-tier travel rewards card due to its straightforward earning rates and no foreign transaction fees. Plus, you have multiple ways to redeem your rewards, including covering recent travel purchases at a fixed rate and transferring your miles to any of the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel partners.

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it an excellent everyday spending card. Plus, it offers 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel. These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards card an appealing and good option for consumers who want to use one card for all their purchases.

Unlike many of the other best everyday spending cards, the Venture Rewards card stands out by offering no foreign transaction fees. The card carries a $95 annual fee but offers a $50 experience credit on every Lifestyle Collection booking, complimentary Hertz Five Star status and up to a $120 statement credit (every four years) when you use your Venture card to apply for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck. Plus, cardholders enjoy price prediction and free price drop protection when booking flights through Capital One Travel.

The Capital One Venture Rewards earns miles that you can redeem for travel, cash back, gift cards, experiences and more. But you can also transfer your miles to 15-plus travel loyalty programs, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Choice Privileges.

Related: 7 reasons to get the Capital One Venture Rewards card

Related: Why I keep the Capital One Venture Rewards card in my wallet

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers cardholders several benefits that help offset the card's $95 annual fee.

One of my favorite benefits of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the price prediction and free price drop protection that's available when I book flights through Capital One Travel.

The price prediction appears anytime you search for a flight through Capital One Travel. It provides guidance on whether to book now and also estimates how pricing is likely to change if you wait to book.

If the price prediction advises booking now, Capital One Travel will automatically apply price drop protection to that purchase at no additional charge. Then, you'll receive up to $50 of the difference back if the price drops within 10 days.

These two features often give me the confidence I need to book or continue to track prices. I've gotten money back on several flights via the automated price drop protection, which is always a nice surprise.

You also have some protection if you book a flight, hotel or rental car through Capital One Travel and then find a better price for the same flight, hotel or rental car on another site within 24 hours of booking. Specifically, you can call Capital One Travel, submit a price match claim and then get a travel credit for the difference if the agent can verify the lower price.

I've successfully done price match guarantees for several flights, with the phone calls often taking under 10 minutes. Keep in mind, though, that the itinerary must be an exact match to what you booked on Capital One Travel, and you must submit your claim within 24 hours of making your reservation through Capital One Travel. The price must be in dollars and available to the general public without any coupons, promotions or member discounts.

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders receive up to a $120 statement credit for the application fee for either Global Entry or TSA PreCheck (every four years). The credit will apply to whichever program is applied to first, so consider your application timing if you plan to pay for applications to both programs with your card.

I love having Global Entry, as it lets me get through U.S. immigration queues quickly, and it also gives me TSA PreCheck. I'd pay the Global Entry application fee even if my Capital One Venture Rewards card didn't offer a statement credit, so this perk effectively gives me up to $120 back (every four years).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders can enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status through the "Benefits" tab of the Capital One website or mobile app. However, it may take up to 72 hours after you register for Hertz status for the upgrade to take effect, so don't wait until you're about to pick up your rental car to register.

I like having Hertz Five Star status, as it provides upgrades when available, 25% more points and a wider choice of vehicles at Ultimate Choice locations.

Each time you make an eligible Lifestyle Collection booking through Capital One Travel, you'll get a $50 experience credit to enjoy during your stay. The booking must be made in the cardholder's name, and the cardholder must be staying on the eligible booking.

If you are staying at a hotel, the hotel will apply the credit at checkout to qualifying charges up to $50. Ask the hotel which purchases qualify, then charge them to your room.

If you're staying at a vacation rental, the host will apply the credit when you book an eligible experience with a Capital One credit card. However, at some vacation rental properties, you may get the experience credit as a gift card.

You'll also enjoy other perks on eligible Lifestyle Collection stays, including complimentary Wi-Fi, early check-in and late checkout. However, early check-in and late checkout are only provided when available, and bookings may have a minimum stay requirement. At hotels, you are also eligible for a room upgrade (subject to availability).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders also get access to Capital One Dining and Capital One Entertainment.

The entertainment platform may be your ticket to cardholder-only VIP packages and hard-to-secure tickets to popular games, concerts and shows.

Meanwhile, the dining platform can help you secure hard-to-get reservations at top restaurants and provide access to exclusive dining events.

Related: Is the Capital One Venture Rewards card worth it?

Capital One miles are easy to earn and redeem yet still offer significant value. Here's what you should know about earning and redeeming Capital One miles.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers simple-to-remember earning rates. Specifically, you'll earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases.

These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards an excellent option, whether it's your only card or you use it primarily for purchases that wouldn't earn bonus rewards on other cards. I often use my Capital One Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar spent if I used another rewards credit card.

One of the big positives of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the flexibility of its miles. However, the two best ways to redeem Capital One miles are to cover recent travel purchases and to transfer miles to select airline or hotel loyalty programs.

Redeeming Capital One miles to cover recent travel purchases gives you 1 cent per mile and is incredibly easy. Once you make an eligible travel purchase with your card, you'll have 90 days to log into the Capital One app or website and redeem rewards to cover your purchase.

However, I prefer to redeem my miles by transferring them to the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel program partners. Some of my favorite options include Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Air Canada Aeroplan and Avianca LifeMiles, but you also have access to JetBlue TrueBlue, Wyndham Rewards and many other programs.

I recently redeemed 80,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points (plus $85 in taxes and fees) to fly business class from Cape Town to Perth, Australia, on an itinerary that would have otherwise cost over $2,200.

As long as you get more than 1 cent per mile when transferring miles to partners, this is the most valuable redemption option. However, TPG's November 2026 valuations peg the value of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents each. So, you'll usually want to choose airline or hotel programs that offer at least this much value for your miles when you transfer them.

Related: Have the Capital One Venture Rewards Card but new to points and miles? Here’s what you need to know

The Capital One Venture Rewards won't be the right card for everyone. Here are some drawbacks to keep in mind:

If the lack of airport lounge benefits and potential difficulty in offsetting the annual fee are your primary concerns about the Capital One Venture, it may be worth considering the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card instead.

The Capital One Venture X has a higher annual fee ($395) than the Venture ($95), but it offers $300 in annual credits toward bookings made through Capital One Travel. Therefore, if you can naturally use the Venture X's full $300 annual Capital One Travel credit, it can effectively narrow the difference between the cards' annual fees to $0.

Venture X cardholders also get 10,000 bonus miles on each account anniversary, starting with the first anniversary. Between the bonus miles and the annual travel credit, most consumers will get more value than the card's annual fee each year.

Plus, the Venture X offers 10 miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel, 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases. Capital One Venture X cardholders also get access to Priority Pass lounges and Capital One lounges.

Choose the Capital One Venture X if you prioritize:

Choose the Capital One Venture Rewards if you prioritize:

Related: Capital One Venture Rewards vs. Capital One Venture X: Worth the extra $300?

A 75,000-mile bonus on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is a solid benchmark. Capital One has also advertised targeted offers of up to 100,000 miles at select airports.

As such, the current welcome offer is worth considering: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. Plus, receive a $300 credit to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year upon account opening. This offer ends soon.

This is one of the best offers we've seen for this card, and this is your last chance to take advantage of it. According to TPG's valuations, this welcome offer is worth $1,688, including the credit.

Note that Capital One won't approve you for a new Capital One Venture Rewards card if you opened a Venture Rewards or Venture X card and earned a bonus in the last 48 months. So, you'll need to wait at least 48 months after earning a welcome bonus on either of these cards before you apply for the Capital One Venture Rewards.

Related: Are you eligible for the Capital One Venture Rewards’ welcome bonus?

If the Capital One Venture Rewards isn't right for you, here are a few other cards to consider:

For other options, read our story on the best starter travel credit cards.

Related: How to pick the right travel credit card for you

I've kept the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card in my wallet for more than a decade because it doesn't require much work to get value from it.

Its 2-mile-per-dollar earning rate makes it useful for purchases that don't earn bonuses on my other cards, while Capital One's transfer partners give me the option to pursue higher-value travel redemptions.

The Venture Rewards isn't the right choice if you want airport lounge access or extensive annual credits. But if you value simplicity, flexible rewards and a reasonable $95 annual fee, it remains a strong mid-tier travel card.

#5974. American Airlines Pilots And Flight Attendants Unite To Demand New Leadership—Say They’re Done Asking Management To Do Better

Five days after American Airlines announced it was replacing Chief Operating Officer, the flight attendants and pilots unions say that change at the top needs to go further. And they’re making this case in part based on American’s poor recovery from this month’s FAA nationwide ground stop. Captain Nick Silva of the Allied Pilots Association and Julie Hedrick of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants signed a joint letter that both unions sent out. They tell management, “We have spent years asking you to do better. Those days are over.” A few lines later they say what they want. “American Airlines needs a new direction — and leadership capable of delivering it.”

Captain Nick Silva of the Allied Pilots Association and Julie Hedrick of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants signed a joint letter that both unions sent out. They tell management, “We have spent years asking you to do better. Those days are over.” A few lines later they say what they want.

“American Airlines needs a new direction — and leadership capable of delivering it.”

In February, the flight attendants’ union board voted unanimously that it had no confidence in Robert Isom. Pilots did not go as far.

And today’s note is being misinterpreted by some as a call for Isom to go. Today’s letter leaves his name out of it, never naming him at all. It’s actually a weaker call than they made earlier in the year.

This gives the unions room to claim a win even if Isom stays CEO. As I wrote earlier today, American may be looking for an outside president who could eventually succeed Isom, and former Wall Street Journal airline reporter Scott McCartney says a hire could come by year-end.

The unions circulated FlightAware data compiled by BofA Global Research. On Saturday, American canceled 42% of its mainline flights, Delta 28% and United 26%. By Sunday, Delta was down to 5%. However, The chart is misleading by picking only two U.S. airlines and mainline flights only. JetBlue cancelled 44% of flights over the 3 days. They left JetBlue off the chart. Including regional flights, American, United and Delta all performed similarly – American cancelled 28.5%, Delta 25.1%, and United 23%. So the union heads are cherry picking by focusing only on mainline. (American even owns three of its regional carriers.) After Winter Storm Fern at the start of the year, I obtained minutes from a flight attendants’ union executive committee meeting. Hedrick said American sent crews to a service center that couldn’t actually book hotel rooms. What struck me at the time was how much sympathy she had for management. On November 15, her union reported that flight attendants waited hours to get their trip assignments fixed, then waited again for rooms. Some never got one. American needed those same people rested to fly passengers the next day. The unions take a swipe in their note at American investing in better seats and lounges. They need those to generate more revenue. Silva himself said in September he wished American had started investing in customers years earlier. What Each Union Gets Out Of Signing Hedrick’s union is helping members claim compensation for hotel delays and get their expenses reimbursed. Having pilots back them publicly helps her bargaining position. She comes out looking tough, even though the note doesn’t go nearly as far as the union went in calling for leadership change earlier in the year. Silva gets a second union making his case that the people who fly the schedule know where it breaks. He opened contract talks a year early and asked for a seat on American’s board. When the pilots asked to make their case to the directors in February, the board sent them back to management. Weak profits are hurting employees. American paid 0.3% of eligible 2025 earnings in profit sharing. On $50,000 that’s $150. At Delta the same earnings would’ve meant $4,450. American already pays competitive pilot wages. I’d expect this negotiation to focus on quality of life issues rather than big raises. But the union is positioning itself to argue that management is at fault for poor performance, shouldn’t get to use that as an excuse for being unable to afford contract concessions, and the union is in fact part of the answer. United pilots got board representation in a 1994 employee buyout involving wage and work rule concessions. They kept it through bankruptcy as part of $1.1 billion in concessions. Delta pilots gained a voting seat in the Northwest merger deal. American’s pilots don’t have a transaction like that to bargain over. Meanwhile, the fight inside their independent union over joining the larger Air Line Pilots Association helped cost Silva’s predecessor his job. Silva wants to show effectiveness taking on management to keep his job.. Another pretty scathing letter put out by the Flight Attendants and Pilots Union at AA calling for new leadership — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 25, 2026 I wrote back in February that the unions would want credit for any change they saw coming. If American names a president in the coming weeks, Silva and Hedrick get to claim a victory and they’ve laid down a marker for what that leader needs to focus on.
